lessons.title: The developer toolkit
lessons.summaryHtml:
AB-400: Power Platform Developer replaces PL-400. You can register for PL-400 until 16 October 2026 and sit it until 30 October 2026. AB-400 is available from 16 October 2026. The passing score is 700, and associate certifications renew yearly with a free online assessment.

A Power Platform developer extends what makers build. You write plug-ins in C#, client scripts and PCF components in TypeScript, code apps, Azure Functions, custom connectors and code-first agents.

  • VS Code with the Power Platform Tools extension is your main editor. The extension also gives you the pac CLI.
  • The .NET SDK builds plug-ins and runs pac as a .NET tool. Node.js builds PCF components and code apps.
  • pac auth create connects pac to an environment. The Plug-in Registration Tool registers plug-ins, steps, images and service endpoints.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A maker builds with the designers in the browser. A developer goes further. You write code that the designers cannot produce: C# plug-ins that run inside Dataverse, TypeScript controls, client scripts, code apps, Azure Functions and custom connectors.

Think of a carpenter. The maker uses ready-made flat-pack furniture. The developer has a workshop with power tools. This lesson sets up that workshop, so every later lesson just works.

It also explains the exam itself. AB-400: Power Platform Developer is the new developer exam. It replaces PL-400, and it adds newer topics such as code apps, MCP servers, Microsoft Foundry agents and managed identity for plug-ins.

Why it matters

Most failed developer projects do not fail because of hard code. They fail because of a broken setup: the wrong environment, an expired sign-in, a missing SDK or a tool that cannot see the solution. The exam also tests the tools directly. You must know which command or tool does which job.

The dates matter if you are planning when to sit the exam.

EventDate
Last day to register for PL-40016 October 2026
Last day to take PL-400 if registered in time30 October 2026
AB-400 availableFrom 16 October 2026

The passing score is 700. Like other associate certifications, it renews every year with a free online assessment on Microsoft Learn.

What you should already know. Microsoft aims AB-400 at developers who work with JavaScript, JSON, TypeScript, Power Fx, C#, Python, HTML, YAML, REST APIs, Azure, Microsoft Foundry and Copilot Studio. You do not need to be an expert in all of them. You should be comfortable reading C# and TypeScript, calling a REST API and editing a YAML file. You should also know the PL-900 basics: environments, Dataverse tables, solutions, canvas and model-driven apps, flows and agents.

How it works

Your toolkit has six parts. Each one has a clear job.

ToolWhat it doesUsed for
Visual Studio CodeCode editor with a built-in terminalEverything: PCF, client scripts, code apps, YAML
Power Platform Tools extensionInstalls pac CLI in VS Code and adds a panel for auth profiles and environmentsSwitching environments, running pac
pac CLICommand-line tool for Power PlatformAuth, solutions, PCF, plug-in projects, code apps
.NET SDKCompiler and build tools for C#Plug-ins, custom API code, Azure Functions
Node.js and npmJavaScript runtime and package managerPCF components, code apps, TypeScript builds
Plug-in Registration ToolWindows desktop tool that talks to DataverseRegistering assemblies, steps, images, service endpoints

Installing pac CLI. There are two common ways. The Power Platform Tools extension installs pac for use inside VS Code. You can also install it as a .NET global tool, which works on Windows, macOS and Linux. The launchers for Windows desktop tools, such as the Plug-in Registration Tool, only work with the Windows (.NET Framework) build of pac.

dotnet tool install --global Microsoft.PowerApps.CLI.Tool
pac                      # shows the help and version

Authentication. pac never guesses an environment. You create an auth profile, which is a saved sign-in linked to one environment URL. You can keep many profiles and switch between them.

pac auth create --environment https://chd-dev.crm.dynamics.com
pac auth list            # shows profiles; * marks the active one
pac auth select --index 2
pac org who              # confirms environment and user

For automation you can sign in with a service principal (an app registration in Microsoft Entra ID) instead of a person. You will use this later for CI/CD.

What pac can do. The commands you will use most in this course:

  • pac solution export, import, unpack, pack and clone move solutions and put them in source control.
  • pac pcf init and pac pcf push create and deploy PCF components.
  • pac plugin init creates a plug-in class library project.
  • pac tool prt launches the Plug-in Registration Tool on Windows.

The .NET SDK and Node.js. Plug-ins are C# class libraries that run in the Dataverse sandbox, so you need the .NET SDK to build them. PCF components and code apps are built with npm scripts, so you need Node.js. Use the LTS release of Node.js.

The Plug-in Registration Tool. Building a plug-in only makes a DLL file. Dataverse does not run it until you register it. The tool uploads the assembly, then adds a step: which message (Create, Update), which table, which pipeline stage, and whether it runs synchronously. It also registers images (snapshots of the row) and service endpoints such as webhooks and Azure Service Bus.

Remember: pac works against the active auth profile. Many “my solution is missing” problems are just the wrong profile selected.

Example: Campus Help Desk

You join the Help Desk team as the developer. Your first day plan:

  1. Install VS Code, the Power Platform Tools extension, the .NET SDK and Node.js LTS.
  2. Run pac auth create --environment https://chd-dev.crm.dynamics.com. Then do the same for the test environment. You now have two profiles.
  3. Run pac auth select to pick dev, then pac solution list. You see Campus Help Desk with the chd publisher prefix.
  4. Export and unpack it into a Git folder so the team can review changes as files: 
    pac solution export --name CampusHelpDesk --path ./out/chd.zip
pac solution unpack --zipfile ./out/chd.zip --folder ./src/CampusHelpDesk
  5. Create the plug-in project for the priority rule you will write in D.9: pac plugin init in a new folder, then dotnet build.
  6. Launch pac tool prt, connect to dev, and look at the registered assemblies. Nothing is there yet. That is where your priority plug-in will go.

Your workshop is ready. The same setup serves the PCF star-rating control, the custom API chd_EscalateTicket and the staff dashboard code app.

Common mistakes

  • Running pac against the wrong environment. Always check pac org who before an import.
  • Thinking a built DLL is live. A plug-in does nothing until it is registered with a step.
  • Skipping Node.js and then wondering why npm run build fails in a PCF project.
  • Expecting the Plug-in Registration Tool on macOS. It is a Windows desktop tool. Plan a Windows machine or VM for registration work.
  • Mixing up the exams. After 30 October 2026 you cannot take PL-400. Study for AB-400, which adds code apps, MCP and Foundry topics.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Connect”, “sign in”, “target a different environment” with pac → pac auth create or pac auth select.
  • “Register a step”, “add a pre-image”, “register a webhook” → Plug-in Registration Tool.
  • “Put the solution in source control as files” → export, then pac solution unpack; the reverse is pack.
  • “Which prerequisite is missing” scenarios → .NET SDK for plug-ins, Node.js for PCF and code apps.

lessons.title: Technical architecture decisions
lessons.summaryHtml:
Architecture is choosing where each piece of work runs before you write code. First ask whether out-of-the-box features already meet the requirement. Code is the last resort, not the first.

  • Business logic can live in business rules, client scripts, plug-ins, cloud flows, Azure services or agents. Each has a different timing, reach and cost.
  • Data can be standard tables, virtual tables (data stays outside Dataverse), elastic tables (very high volume) or plain connectors.
  • Security features such as managed environments, data policies, security roles, teams, business units and row sharing shape your design.
  • Deterministic logic gives the same result every time. Non-deterministic logic, such as AI or agents, can vary, so keep strict rules in code.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Technical architecture means deciding where each piece of work lives before anyone writes code. Should a rule run in the browser or on the server? During the save or after it? In a flow, in a plug-in or in an agent?

Think of building a house. You decide where the plumbing and wiring go before the walls go up. Moving them later is expensive. The same is true for business logic.

For a developer, architecture is also about restraint. Every plug-in, script and function you add must be tested, deployed, monitored and maintained for years. A good architect writes the least code that meets the requirement, and puts each piece where it is cheapest to run and easiest to trust.

Why it matters

The Campus Help Desk grew fast. A rule written as a client script only runs on one form, so tickets created from the canvas app skip it. A heavy SLA check written as a synchronous plug-in makes every save slow. A due date calculated by an AI prompt changes from one run to the next. Each is a wrong architecture choice, not a coding bug. AB-400 tests these choices heavily.

How it works

Step 1: can out-of-the-box features meet the need? Check business rules, formula columns, views, security roles and standard connectors first. Code costs more to build, test and maintain.

Step 2: choose where logic runs.

OptionRunsBest forLimits
Business ruleForm, and server for table-scope rulesSimple show, hide, require, set valueNo external calls, simple conditions
Client scriptBrowser, on the formInstant form feedback, notificationsSkipped by imports, API calls and canvas apps
Synchronous plug-inServer, inside the transactionValidation and data changes for every channelMust be fast; slows every save
Asynchronous plug-inServer, after the saveFollow-up work, external callsUser does not see the result at once
Azure FunctionAzureLong-running, scheduled or event-driven jobsMore infrastructure to run
Cloud flowPower AutomateNotifications, approvals, connector workNot for blocking saves
Copilot Studio agentCopilot StudioConversations, knowledge, reasoningNon-deterministic output

Step 3: choose where data lives.

  • Standard tables for normal business data with full Dataverse features.
  • Virtual tables when data must stay in another system but appear in Dataverse.
  • Elastic tables for very high volume, fast-changing data such as logs and sensor readings.
  • Connectors when an app or flow just needs to call a system, without a table.

Step 4: authentication and authorization. Authentication proves who you are, usually with Microsoft Entra ID. Authorization decides what you may do. In Dataverse that is security roles, business units, teams and row sharing. Your code runs under a user or an app identity, and it must respect these rules. For services, prefer a service principal or managed identity over stored passwords.

Step 5: governance. Managed environments add admin controls, and data policies decide which connectors can be used together. A design that needs a blocked connector will fail in production, so check policies early.

Step 6: deterministic or not. A plug-in always gives the same answer. An AI prompt or agent may not. Keep rules, money and deadlines deterministic. Use AI where judgement helps, such as suggesting a category.

Step 7: choose the user experience.

  • Generative pages: a model-driven page built from a natural-language description.
  • PCF components: reusable custom controls on forms, views and canvas apps.
  • Web resources: JavaScript, HTML or images stored in Dataverse, used by forms and commands.
  • Code apps: a full custom web app, such as React and TypeScript, hosted on Power Platform.
  • Interactive agents and MCP app widgets: UI surfaced inside agent conversations.

Step 8: which agent platform. Copilot Studio is low-code, fast and close to Power Platform. Microsoft Foundry is code-first, for custom models, orchestration and deep engineering control. The two can connect.

Watch out: a client script is not security. Anyone can create a row through the Web API and skip it. Rules that must never be broken belong on the server.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The team gives you five requirements. Here is the design.

  1. Priority from keywords on every new ticket. Synchronous plug-in on Create, PreOperation stage. It runs for the canvas app, the staff app and imports.
  2. Warn staff on the form when a category has many open tickets. Client script on the Category change event, using Xrm.WebApi.retrieveMultipleRecords.
  3. Nightly SLA check. Azure Function with a timer trigger, signing in with a managed identity.
  4. Email the student when a ticket closes. Cloud flow on the Dataverse trigger with a filter on Status.
  5. Students ask how-to questions. The Help Desk Assistant agent in Copilot Studio.

Student records stay in the Campus Directory, so you plan a custom connector to its API rather than copying the data. Every part lives in the Campus Help Desk solution with the chd prefix.

Common mistakes

  • Coding first. A business rule or formula column is often enough.
  • Using a client script for validation that must apply to every channel.
  • Putting slow work in a synchronous plug-in, so every save waits for an external API.
  • Trusting AI for fixed rules such as deadlines or prices.
  • Ignoring data policies until deployment, when a connector turns out to be blocked.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Regardless of how the record is created”, “must prevent the save” → synchronous plug-in.
  • “Without delaying the user”, “long-running”, “nightly” → asynchronous plug-in or Azure Function.
  • “Data must remain in the external system” → virtual table or connector. “Millions of rows, high throughput” → elastic table.
  • “Same result every time” → deterministic logic, not a prompt or agent.

terms.definition: Runs inside the Dataverse transaction. It can block or change the save and roll it back on error.
Runs after the save, in the background, through the asynchronous service. It does not slow the user.
A Dataverse table whose rows live in an external system and are read through a data provider.
A Dataverse table type built for very large, fast-changing data sets such as logs or telemetry.
Logic that always produces the same output for the same input, such as a plug-in rule.

lessons.examTip: “Must run on every save, from any client, and block bad data” points to a synchronous plug-in. “Only on the form, instant feedback” points to a client script.

sorter.title: Where should this logic live?
sorter.intro: Pick the best place for each Campus Help Desk requirement.

items.t: Make Due date required when Priority is High, on the form, with no code.
items.w: A simple show, hide, require or set-value rule on a form is exactly what business rules do without code.

items.t: When a staff member changes Category on the form, call the Web API and show a notification listing open tickets in that category.
items.w: This is form-only, interactive behaviour that needs the Client API and Web API, so a client script fits.

items.t: Block saving any ticket whose Title contains banned words, from every client and every import.
items.w: Only a synchronous plug-in runs for every channel and can stop the transaction with an error.

items.t: Every night, check thousands of open tickets against SLA dates and mark breaches.
items.w: Long, scheduled, heavy work belongs outside the user transaction, such as an Azure Function with a timer trigger.

items.t: When a ticket closes, email the student and post a message in the staff Teams channel.
items.w: Notifications across Outlook and Teams are a classic cloud flow with standard connectors.

items.t: Students ask in plain language how to reset their Wi-Fi password and get an answer from the knowledge base.
items.w: Conversational, knowledge-grounded answers are the job of a Copilot Studio agent.

items.t: After a ticket is created, call the Campus Directory API to fill the student’s department. The user should not wait.
items.w: The call is to an external service and can run after the save, so an asynchronous plug-in or a function fits.

items.t: Route a new High priority ticket for manager approval before it is assigned.
items.w: Approvals are built into cloud flows with the Approvals connector.

lessons.title: Designing solution components
lessons.summaryHtml:
After the architecture, you design each component so it is reusable, secure and easy to monitor. AB-400 expects you to know which component fits which job.

  • User experience: generative pages, PCF code components, client scripts and code apps for fully custom interfaces.
  • Dataverse code: plug-ins react to events. Custom APIs add your own messages, such as chd_EscalateTicket.
  • Connectivity: custom connectors and MCP servers expose APIs to apps, flows and agents.
  • Automation and agents: cloud flows, Copilot Studio workflows and custom agents.
  • Integration and monitoring: inbound and outbound integration with Azure, plus Application Insights and Power Platform monitor alerts.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Architecture decided where things run. Component design decides what each piece looks like: its inputs, outputs, security and how you will watch it in production.

Think of LEGO. A good brick has a standard shape, so you can use it in many models. A good Power Platform component is the same. You build it once and reuse it in apps, flows and agents.

Why it matters

Without design, teams copy logic. The escalation rule ends up in a flow, a form script and an agent topic, each slightly different. When the rule changes, one copy is missed. Good component design gives one source of truth and makes failures visible.

How it works

AB-400 groups components into six families.

FamilyComponentsDesign questions
Reusable UIGenerative pages, PCF, client scriptsWhere is it reused? What data does it bind to?
ConnectivityCustom connectors, MCP serversWhat authentication? Which operations?
Dataverse codePlug-ins, custom APIsWhich message and stage? What inputs and outputs?
AutomationCloud flows, Copilot Studio workflowsWhat trigger? How are errors handled?
Custom interfaces and agentsCode apps, custom agentsWho signs in? What data and tools do they use?
Integration and monitoringAzure services, Application Insights, monitor alertsInbound or outbound? How do we know it failed?

Reusable UI. A PCF component is a TypeScript control with a manifest that declares its properties. It is reused across forms, views and canvas apps. Client scripts should live in one web resource per area, with small named functions registered as event handlers. Generative pages are fast to create from a description; treat them as components that still need review and testing.

Custom connectors and MCP servers. A custom connector wraps a REST API using an OpenAPI definition. Apps, flows and agents all call it. An MCP server exposes tools through the Model Context Protocol. An agent reads the tool list from the server, so new operations appear without redesigning the agent. Use a connector for apps and flows; add an MCP server when agents must discover tools.

Plug-ins and custom APIs. A plug-in reacts to an existing message such as Create or Update. A custom API creates a new message with its own name, request parameters and response properties. A plug-in usually implements it. A custom API can be:

  • Unbound or bound to a table (acts on one row) or an entity collection.
  • An action (can change data, called with POST) or a function (reads only, called with GET).
  • Private, so only your own code can call it.
POST [org]/api/data/v9.2/chd_tickets(<ticketid>)/Microsoft.Dynamics.CRM.chd_EscalateTicket
{ "Reason": "No reply after 48 hours" }

Automations. Cloud flows handle notifications, approvals and connector work. Copilot Studio workflows (agent flows) are deterministic flows that agents call. Design both with clear triggers, filters and error handling, and call shared logic through custom APIs or child flows.

Integrations. Inbound means other systems send data to Dataverse, for example through the Web API. Outbound means Dataverse tells others, for example by posting events to Azure Service Bus or a webhook. Azure Functions often sit in between to transform data.

Custom interfaces and agents. A code app is a pro-code web app, such as React and TypeScript, that runs on Power Platform. It uses connectors and Dataverse through generated client libraries, and it gets Entra sign-in, sharing and governance. Custom agents can be built in Copilot Studio or in Microsoft Foundry.

Monitoring and alerting. Design monitoring from day one:

  • Plug-ins write trace messages with ITracingService, visible in the plug-in trace log.
  • Dataverse and apps can send telemetry to Application Insights, where you query failures and set alert rules.
  • Power Platform monitor in the admin center shows health metrics, and you can configure alerts there.
Remember: if the same business operation is needed from several places, make it a custom API. Everything else calls that one API.

Example: Campus Help Desk

You write a component design for the next release.

  1. chd_EscalateTicket custom API. Bound to Ticket, an action. Input Reason (string). Output NewOwnerId. A plug-in implements it. Called by a command button, a flow and the agent.
  2. Star-rating PCF control. Bound to a whole-number column chd_feedbackrating. Used on the staff form and in the student canvas app.
  3. Campus Directory custom connector. Imported from the API’s OpenAPI file, OAuth 2.0 with Entra ID. Operation: GetStudent.
  4. Help Desk MCP server. Exposes “find ticket” and “escalate ticket” tools for a Foundry agent.
  5. Staff dashboard code app. React and TypeScript, reads tickets from Dataverse and calls the connector.
  6. Monitoring. Plug-ins trace every decision. Telemetry flows to Application Insights with an alert when escalation failures spike.

Each component has one owner, one purpose and a clear way to see failure.

Common mistakes

  • Copying logic into every client instead of one custom API.
  • Using a custom action workflow for new work; custom APIs are the modern way to define messages.
  • Building a web resource per form when one PCF component could serve all apps.
  • Adding monitoring after go-live, when the first failure is already hidden.
  • Storing secrets in code instead of using managed identity, Key Vault or connector authentication.

How the exam asks about it

  • “New message”, “callable from Web API, flows and agents”, “typed inputs and outputs” → custom API.
  • “Reusable control in model-driven and canvas apps” → PCF component.
  • “Agent must discover tools” → MCP server. “Flow or app calls a REST API” → custom connector.
  • “Alert operations”, “query telemetry” → Application Insights or Power Platform monitor alerts.

terms.definition: Your own Dataverse message with defined inputs and outputs, callable from the Web API, flows and code, often backed by a plug-in.
A reusable TypeScript UI control built with the Power Apps component framework, used in model-driven and canvas apps.
A wrapper around a REST API, described by an OpenAPI definition, so apps, flows and agents can call it.
A server using the Model Context Protocol that offers tools an agent can discover and call.
An Azure Monitor service that collects telemetry, errors and performance data from apps and Dataverse.

lessons.examTip: “Reusable business operation callable from a flow, the Web API and an agent” means a custom API. “Reusable UI control” means PCF.

lessons.title: ALM and CI/CD for developers
lessons.summaryHtml:
ALM (application lifecycle management) moves your work safely from development to test to production. As a developer you manage what a solution depends on, what changes per environment, and how layers stack.

  • Solution dependencies stop a solution from importing when a component it needs is missing.
  • Environment variables hold values that differ per environment, such as the Campus Directory API URL.
  • Solution layers: managed solutions stack as layers; unmanaged changes form the active layer on top, which wins at runtime.
  • Power Platform Pipelines give in-product deployments, which you can extend with approvals and custom steps.
  • Power Platform Build Tools for Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions give full CI/CD in source control.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

ALM stands for application lifecycle management. It is the path your work takes from your development environment to test and then to production, without breaking anything on the way.

Think of a restaurant. Chefs try new dishes in the test kitchen. Only a finished, written recipe goes to the main kitchen, and nobody changes it there on the fly. Dev is the test kitchen. A managed solution is the written recipe. Production is the main kitchen.

Why it matters

A developer’s changes touch plug-ins, PCF controls, connectors and flows. If a deployment misses a dependency, the import fails. If a URL is hard-coded, test calls the production API. If someone edits production directly, your next release seems to do nothing. AB-400 tests how to prevent each of these.

How it works

1. Solution dependencies. A component often needs another one. A flow needs its connection reference. A form needs its columns. A plug-in step needs its table. Dataverse tracks these as dependencies. When you import, every required component must be in the solution or already in the target. If not, the import fails and lists what is missing.

  • Use Show dependencies on a component to see what it needs and what needs it.
  • Dependencies also block deletes: you cannot remove a column a view still uses.
  • Split big systems into layered solutions, for example a core data solution and an app solution that depends on it. Deploy the core first.

2. Environment variables. An environment variable has a definition (name, type, default value) and an optional current value per environment. Types include text, decimal number, JSON, yes/no, data source and secret (backed by Azure Key Vault). Apps, flows, plug-ins and code apps read the value at runtime.

When you deploy, you supply each environment’s value. With pac, pac solution create-settings builds a deployment settings JSON file listing environment variables and connection references. Pipelines ask for the values during deployment.

3. Solution layers. Each managed solution you install adds a layer for its components. Unmanaged changes sit in the active layer on top.

LayerComes fromBehaviour
SystemDataverse itselfBase definitions
Managed layersEach managed solution, in install orderA later layer overrides an earlier one
Active (unmanaged)Direct edits and unmanaged solutionsAlways on top; wins at runtime

For most components the top layer wins. Some, such as forms and site maps, merge changes from several layers. To see the stack, open a component and choose See solution layers. To drop unmanaged edits so the managed version shows again, use Remove active customizations.

4. Power Platform Pipelines. Pipelines bring ALM into the product. An admin sets up a host environment that stores pipeline definitions. A pipeline links a development source to one or more stages, such as Test and Production. Makers and developers deploy from the solution screen. Pipelines deploy managed solutions, check dependencies, ask for environment variable values and keep a history. Target environments must be managed environments.

Extending pipelines. You can switch on gated extensions for a stage:

  • Pre-export step required: run checks before the solution is exported.
  • Pre-deployment step required: pause before import, for example for an approval or security scan.
  • Is delegated deployment: deploy as a service principal or a stage owner rather than the requester.

Pipelines also raise events such as OnDeploymentRequested, OnApprovalStarted, OnPreDeploymentStarted and OnDeploymentCompleted. A cloud flow can trigger on these events, do custom work, and then mark the gated step as complete or rejected. Approval and pre-deployment events only fire when the matching extension is enabled.

5. Power Platform Build Tools and GitHub Actions. For full CI/CD with source control, use Power Platform Build Tools in Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions for Power Platform. Both wrap pac. Typical tasks: install tools, export, unpack, check, pack and import. Sign in with a service principal through a service connection or secrets. A short Azure DevOps example:

steps:
- task: PowerPlatformToolInstaller@2
- task: PowerPlatformExportSolution@2
  inputs:
    authenticationType: PowerPlatformSPN
    PowerPlatformSPN: 'chd-dev-connection'
    SolutionName: 'CampusHelpDesk'
    SolutionOutputFile: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/chd.zip'
    Managed: false
- task: PowerPlatformUnpackSolution@2
  inputs:
    SolutionInputFile: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/chd.zip'
    SolutionTargetFolder: 'src/CampusHelpDesk'

In GitHub the matching steps use actions such as microsoft/powerplatform-actions/export-solution, unpack-solution, pack-solution and import-solution, with app-id, client-secret and tenant-id for the service principal.

Watch out: never deploy unmanaged solutions to production. You lose clean removal and you create an active layer that hides later managed updates.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. You add environment variable chd_DirectoryApiUrl to the solution. The custom connector and the Azure Function read it.
  2. Show dependencies on the escalation flow reveals it needs the Campus Directory connection reference. You add it to the solution.
  3. A nightly Azure DevOps pipeline exports the unmanaged solution from dev, unpacks it into Git, and runs the solution checker. Reviewers see plug-in and form changes as file diffs.
  4. For releases, staff use a Power Platform pipeline: Dev → Test → Production. The Production stage has the pre-deployment gated extension on.
  5. When OnPreDeploymentStarted fires, a cloud flow posts an approval to the Help Desk manager. Approved means the step is completed and import continues.
  6. In test, the new Ticket form does not appear. See solution layers shows an active layer from a quick manual fix. You remove active customizations and the managed form appears.

Common mistakes

  • Hard-coding URLs and keys instead of environment variables.
  • Forgetting dependencies such as connection references, then failing the import.
  • Editing managed components in production, creating an active layer that hides releases.
  • Using a personal account in CI/CD. Use a service principal so deployments do not break when a person leaves.
  • Keeping only zip files in source control; unpack them so changes can be reviewed.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Import fails, component missing” → dependency; add it or deploy the base solution first.
  • “Value differs per environment” → environment variable, supplied through deployment settings or pipelines.
  • “Change not visible after managed update” → active layer; remove active customizations.
  • “Approval or external check before deploy” → pipelines gated extension with a flow. “Source control, YAML, pull requests” → Build Tools or GitHub Actions.

terms.definition: A locked, deployable package for test and production. Removing it removes its components.
The unmanaged layer on top of all managed layers. Its changes win at runtime.
A solution component with a definition and a value, so settings can change per environment without editing the app.

An app identity in Microsoft Entra ID used by pipelines and CI/CD to sign in without a person.

lessons.examTip: “Change I made in production is hiding my new managed version” means an unmanaged active layer. Remove active customizations.

lessons.title: Client scripting in model-driven apps
lessons.summaryHtml:
Client scripting means JavaScript that runs in the browser on model-driven forms and grids. You load it as a JavaScript web resource, attach functions to events such as OnLoad, OnChange and OnSave, and work through the Client API object model.

  • Always start from the execution context: executionContext.getFormContext() gives the form. Xrm.Page is deprecated.
  • Xrm.WebApi reads and writes Dataverse rows from script; it calls the Dataverse Web API for you.
  • Xrm.Navigation opens dialogs and forms; formContext.ui.setFormNotification and control notifications show messages.
  • Command bar buttons can be built in the command designer with Power Fx or with a JavaScript action.

Use script for instant, user-facing behaviour. Rules that must always hold belong on the server (plug-ins), because script only runs when someone uses the form.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A model-driven form is like a paper form with a helpful clerk standing beside it. Client scripting is the clerk. When the form opens, when a field changes, or when someone presses Save, your JavaScript can react: show a message, hide a field, fill a value or check data before it goes to the server.

The script lives in a JavaScript web resource, a file stored in Dataverse and shipped inside your solution. You attach functions from that file to form events. The platform then calls your function and hands it an execution context, which is your door into the form.

Why it matters

Help desk staff want instant feedback. If they set Priority to High, they should see at once that a Due date is required. Waiting for a server error after Save is slow and annoying. Client script gives that instant, on-screen help.

But script only runs in the browser, and only in the form where you registered it. A cloud flow, an Excel import or the Web API never runs it. So the golden rule for the exam is: use client script for user experience; use server logic (plug-ins, business rules with entity scope, Power Automate) for rules that must always hold.

How it works

The Client API object model has a few main parts:

ObjectWhat it gives youTypical use
executionContextThe event that fired and the formgetFormContext(), getEventArgs() on save
formContext.data / getAttributeColumn values on the rowgetValue(), setValue(), setRequiredLevel("required"), addOnChange()
formContext.ui / getControlWhat the user seessetVisible(), setDisabled(), setNotification(), ui.setFormNotification()
Xrm.WebApiDataverse data from scriptretrieveRecord, retrieveMultipleRecords, createRecord, updateRecord
Xrm.NavigationDialogs and navigationopenAlertDialog, openConfirmDialog, openForm
Xrm.Utility / Xrm.AppHelpers and app-level UIgetGlobalContext(), progress indicators, global notifications

Registering event handlers. There are two main approaches, and you often combine them.

  • In the form designer: add the web resource to the form’s libraries, then register a function on OnLoad, OnSave or a column’s OnChange. Tick Pass execution context as first parameter. Use a namespaced function name such as CHD.Ticket.onLoad so it cannot clash with other scripts.
  • In code: register one OnLoad handler in the designer, then add the rest in code with addOnChange, addOnSave and similar. This keeps all wiring in one file, which is easier to review and move between environments.

Calling the Web API. Xrm.WebApi methods return promises and call the Dataverse Web API (/api/data/v9.2/) for you, with the user’s own permissions. Query options are OData strings such as ?$select=...&$filter=.... A lookup is filtered with its value property, such as _chd_category_value. For calls that Xrm.WebApi does not wrap, you can build the URL from Xrm.Utility.getGlobalContext().getClientUrl() and call the Web API with fetch.

Commands and buttons. The modern command designer lets you add buttons to the main grid, form, subgrid or associated view. Each command has an action and a visibility rule. Both can be written in Power Fx (for example Patch on Self.Selected.Item), or the action can run a JavaScript function from a web resource. Power Fx suits makers and simple data changes; JavaScript suits complex logic or calls to custom APIs.

Notifications and dialogs. Choose the smallest message that works: a control notification next to one field, a form notification across the top of the form, an alert or confirm dialog when the user must react, or a global notification for the whole app.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Goal: when Priority becomes High, require a Due date, warn the user and tell them how many open tickets share the category.

var CHD = window.CHD || {};
CHD.Ticket = {
  HIGH: 100000002, // use the value of High in your choice
  onLoad: function (executionContext) {
    var formContext = executionContext.getFormContext();
    formContext.getAttribute("chd_priority").addOnChange(CHD.Ticket.onPriorityChange);
  },
  onPriorityChange: function (executionContext) {
    var formContext = executionContext.getFormContext();
    var isHigh = formContext.getAttribute("chd_priority").getValue() === CHD.Ticket.HIGH;
    formContext.getAttribute("chd_duedate").setRequiredLevel(isHigh ? "required" : "none");
    if (!isHigh) { formContext.ui.clearFormNotification("chd_high"); return; }
    formContext.ui.setFormNotification("High priority: set a Due date.", "WARNING", "chd_high");
    var cat = formContext.getAttribute("chd_category").getValue();
    if (!cat) { return; }
    var id = cat[0].id.replace(/[{}]/g, "");
    Xrm.WebApi.retrieveMultipleRecords("chd_ticket",
      "?$select=chd_title&$filter=_chd_category_value eq " + id + " and statecode eq 0")
      .then(function (result) {
        Xrm.Navigation.openAlertDialog({ text: result.entities.length + " open tickets in this category." });
      });
  }
};
  1. Save this as chd_/scripts/ticket.js in the Campus Help Desk solution.
  2. On the Ticket main form, add the library and register CHD.Ticket.onLoad on OnLoad with the execution context passed.
  3. Publish, open a ticket, change Priority, and watch the warning and alert.
  4. Add a “Close ticket” command in the command designer with a Power Fx action that patches Status to Closed, visible only when Status is not already Closed.
Remember: lookups come back as an array of objects with id, name and entityType. Choices come back as numbers, not labels.

Common mistakes

  • Using Xrm.Page. It is deprecated; always use the execution context and getFormContext().
  • Touching the page’s HTML (DOM) directly. That is unsupported and breaks when Microsoft changes the UI.
  • Forgetting to tick Pass execution context as first parameter, so executionContext is undefined.
  • Putting security or must-hold rules only in script. Imports, flows and API calls skip it.
  • Global function names without a namespace, which clash with other libraries on the same form.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Immediately”, “as the user types or selects”, “show a message on the form” point to client script on OnChange or OnLoad.
  • “Prevent the save” points to an OnSave handler and getEventArgs().preventDefault().
  • “Regardless of how the row is created” points away from script to a plug-in or other server logic.
  • “Maker with Power Fx skills adds a button” points to a command built in the command designer; “call a custom API from a button” suggests a JavaScript command action.

The object passed to an event handler. It tells you the event and gives you the form through getFormContext().

A file such as JavaScript, HTML or an image stored in Dataverse and shipped inside a solution.

The modern designer for command bar buttons. Actions and visibility can use Power Fx or JavaScript.

lessons.examTip: “Use the execution context” and “Xrm.Page is deprecated” are classic answers. “Must also apply to imports, flows and the API” means the logic belongs in a plug-in, not client script.

quiz.question: A developer copies an old script that uses Xrm.Page.getAttribute("chd_duedate"). What should they change it to?
options: executionContext.getFormContext().getAttribute("chd_duedate"), with the execution context passed to the handler
quiz.explanation: Xrm.Page is deprecated. Handlers receive the execution context and get the form through getFormContext(). DOM access is unsupported.

quiz.question: Staff must not save a ticket whose Due date is in the past when they use the form. Which approach is correct in client script?
options: OnLoad handler that hides the Save button
OnChange handler that deletes the value
OnSave handler that calls executionContext.getEventArgs().preventDefault() and shows a notification
quiz.explanation: OnSave handlers can cancel the save with getEventArgs().preventDefault(). Add a control or form notification so the user knows why.

quiz.question: The rule “High priority tickets must have a Due date” must also apply to rows created by a cloud flow and data imports. Where should it live?
options: A synchronous plug-in (or a server-side rule)
quiz.explanation: Client script only runs in the form. Server-side logic such as a plug-in runs for every channel that writes the row.

quiz.question: A form script needs the list of open tickets in the same category without leaving the page. Which call fits best?
quiz.explanation: Xrm.WebApi.retrieveMultipleRecords queries Dataverse through the Web API and returns a promise with the entities array.

lessons.title: PCF code components
lessons.summaryHtml:
The Power Apps component framework (PCF) lets you build your own controls in TypeScript and use them in model-driven apps, canvas apps and Power Pages. A field component replaces how one column is shown; a dataset component replaces how a view or grid is shown.

  • The manifest (ControlManifest.Input.xml) declares the namespace, properties, resources and features used.
  • The lifecycle is init (once), updateView (whenever data or layout changes), getOutputs (hands values back after you call notifyOutputChanged) and destroy (clean up).
  • The context object gives parameters plus features such as context.webAPI, context.device and context.utils.
  • Tooling: pac pcf init, npm run build, npm start watch for the test harness, pac pcf push for quick dev deployment, and a solution project for proper ALM.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Power Apps comes with a box of standard controls: text boxes, toggles, grids. Sometimes none of them fits. The Power Apps component framework (PCF) lets you build your own control in TypeScript, package it, and drop it onto a form or canvas screen just like a built-in one. Think of it as making your own Lego brick that clicks into the same baseplate.

Why it matters

Campus Help Desk wants students to rate how well a ticket was handled. A number box that says “4” is dull and easy to mistype. A row of clickable stars is clear and friendly. With PCF you build the star control once and reuse it on the staff form, in the student canvas app and in any other app that has a rating column. A client script cannot do this, because script changes an existing form; it does not create a reusable control.

How it works

Two kinds of component.

TemplateBinds toExample
fieldOne column valueStar rating on Satisfaction
datasetA view, subgrid or table of rowsTicket cards instead of a grid

The manifest. ControlManifest.Input.xml describes the component to the platform: its namespace and constructor (class name), version, properties, the code and CSS files, and the platform features it uses. Each property has a type (such as Whole.None or SingleLine.Text) and a usage: bound (linked to a column, read and write), input (a setting the maker types in) or output.

<control namespace="Chd" constructor="StarRating" version="1.0.0"
  display-name-key="Star rating" description-key="Rate 1 to 5" control-type="standard">
  <property name="rating" display-name-key="Rating" of-type="Whole.None" usage="bound" required="true" />
  <property name="maxStars" display-name-key="Max stars" of-type="Whole.None" usage="input" default-value="5" />
  <resources>
    <code path="index.ts" order="1" />
    <css path="css/StarRating.css" order="1" />
  </resources>
</control>

The lifecycle. Your class implements four methods that the framework calls for you:

  1. init(context, notifyOutputChanged, state, container) runs once. Keep the container element and the notifyOutputChanged callback; add event listeners.
  2. updateView(context) runs whenever something changes: the bound value, other properties, the control’s size or disabled state. Redraw here from context.parameters.
  3. getOutputs() runs after you call notifyOutputChanged(). Return the new values for bound or output properties; the platform writes them to the column.
  4. destroy() runs when the control is removed. Remove listeners and timers.
export class StarRating implements ComponentFramework.StandardControl<IInputs, IOutputs> {
  private value = 0;
  private container!: HTMLDivElement;
  private notify!: () => void;
  public init(context: ComponentFramework.Context<IInputs>, notifyOutputChanged: () => void,
    state: ComponentFramework.Dictionary, container: HTMLDivElement): void {
    this.container = container;
    this.notify = notifyOutputChanged;
  }
  public updateView(context: ComponentFramework.Context<IInputs>): void {
    this.value = context.parameters.rating.raw ?? 0;
    // redraw stars; a click sets this.value and calls this.notify()
  }
  public getOutputs(): IOutputs { return { rating: this.value }; }
  public destroy(): void { /* remove click listeners */ }
}

Context features. The context object is your toolbox:

  • context.webAPI: create, read, update and delete Dataverse rows.
  • context.device: capture an image, audio or video, read a barcode, get the location, pick a file.
  • context.utils: helpers such as opening a lookup dialog or reading table metadata.
  • context.navigation, context.formatting, context.resources and context.mode for navigation, number and date formats, localized strings and disabled or visible state.

Features such as WebAPI, Utility and Device.captureImage must be declared in a feature-usage section of the manifest with uses-feature elements.

Virtual (React) components. pac pcf init can create a component that uses the platform’s shared React and Fluent UI libraries, declared as platform libraries in the manifest. The bundle is smaller and loads faster because React is not packed inside your component. Its updateView returns a React element instead of drawing into the container.

Package, deploy, consume.

StepCommand or action
Createpac pcf init --namespace Chd --name StarRating --template field --run-npm-install
Build and testnpm run build, then npm start watch for the test harness
Quick dev deploypac pcf push --publisher-prefix chd (development only)
Proper ALMpac solution init, pac solution add-reference --path ..., then build the solution project to get a zip
Use in model-drivenForm designer: select the column, add the component under Components
Use in canvasThe environment must allow code components in canvas apps; then import it as a code component

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Add a whole number column chd_satisfaction to Ticket, with a range of 1 to 5.
  2. Run pac pcf init with the field template and edit the manifest as shown above.
  3. In updateView, draw five star buttons. Filled stars go up to the current value. Disable them when context.mode.isControlDisabled is true.
  4. On click, set the value and call notifyOutputChanged(). getOutputs returns { rating: value }.
  5. Test with npm start watch, then push with pac pcf push --publisher-prefix chd.
  6. On the Ticket main form, bind the Star rating component to Satisfaction. Later, add the component project to the Campus Help Desk solution project so it moves through Test and Production with the rest.
Watch out: pac pcf push puts the component in a temporary solution in your dev environment. For Test and Production, ship it inside your real solution.

Common mistakes

  • Changing the value without calling notifyOutputChanged, so the column never updates.
  • Doing one-time setup in updateView, which runs many times, and leaking event listeners.
  • Forgetting to bump the version in the manifest, so the environment keeps the old component.
  • Using context.device or context.webAPI without declaring the feature in the manifest.
  • Choosing field when the requirement is about a whole view (that is dataset).

How the exam asks about it

  • “Reusable”, “custom visual control”, “in both model-driven and canvas apps” point to PCF.
  • “Replace the grid for a view” points to a dataset component; “one column” to a field component.
  • Questions list lifecycle methods and ask which runs once, which runs on every change, and which returns values.
  • “Camera”, “barcode”, “location” point to the Device feature declared in the manifest.

terms.definition: A reusable control built with PCF in TypeScript that runs inside Power Apps like a built-in control.
The manifest file that defines the component’s namespace, constructor, properties, resources and feature usage.
A property linked to a column (usage="bound"). The component reads and writes its value.
A callback given in init. Calling it tells the framework to call getOutputs and save the new value.
A local browser page started with npm start watch to try the component without deploying.
A PCF component that uses the platform’s shared React library instead of bundling its own copy.

lessons.examTip: Lifecycle order is a favourite: init once, updateView many times, getOutputs only after notifyOutputChanged, destroy at the end. A manifest change needs a version bump to be picked up.

lessons.title: Build Power Apps code apps
lessons.summaryHtml:
Code apps are web apps you write in a code editor, with frameworks such as React or Vue, that run on Power Platform. You keep full control of the UI and logic, while Power Platform gives you Microsoft Entra sign-in, hosting, connectors, sharing, DLP and Conditional Access.

  • An admin first turns on Power Apps code apps for the environment. You need Node.js LTS, Git and an editor such as VS Code.
  • The npm-based Power Apps CLI (pa) and the client library @microsoft/power-apps do the work: pa app init, pa app run, pa app add data-source, pa app push. The older pac code commands are being replaced by it.
  • Adding a data source generates typed models and services in src/generated. You call methods such as getAll, create and update.
  • You can also add Dataverse actions and functions, instant flows with the Power Apps trigger, Copilot Studio agents and environment variables.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A canvas app is like decorating a flat with the landlord’s furniture: quick, but you use what is provided. A code app is like bringing your own furniture into the same building. You write a normal web app in VS Code with React, Vue or another framework. The building still gives you the security guard (Microsoft Entra sign-in), the keys (sharing), the house rules (DLP, Conditional Access) and the pipes to data (connectors and Dataverse).

Why it matters

Help desk managers want a staff dashboard with custom charts, fast filtering and a layout that no canvas screen can match. Before code apps, a developer would build a separate website and then solve hosting, sign-in and data access alone. With a code app, the developer keeps full control of the UI and logic, and Power Platform handles hosting, identity, connector access and governance. The app appears in Power Apps next to the others, and admins manage it the same way.

How it works

Before you start. An admin turns on Power Apps code apps in the environment’s feature settings in the Power Platform admin center. You install Node.js (LTS), Git and an editor. End users need a Power Apps Premium licence, or the environment uses pay-as-you-go, App Pass or auto-claim.

The tooling. Microsoft now documents an npm-based Power Apps CLI, with commands that start with pa. It replaces the older preview pac code commands in the Power Platform CLI.

TaskPower Apps CLI (current)Older pac command
Set up the app in a folderpa app initpac code init
Run locallypa app runpac code run
Add a connector or tablepa app add data-sourcepac code add-data-source
Publishpa app pushpac code push

The quickstart copies a Vite template, installs the CLI and the client library, then initializes the app:

npx degit github:microsoft/PowerAppsCodeApps/templates/vite chd-staff-dashboard
cd chd-staff-dashboard
npm install --global @microsoft/power-apps-cli
npm install --global @microsoft/power-apps
npm install
pa app init --display-name "Help Desk Staff Dashboard" --environment-id <environment-id>
pa app run

pa app run prints a Local Play URL. Open it in the same browser profile you use for Power Platform. Chrome and Edge may ask for permission because a public site is calling a local address.

Architecture. Three layers work together: your single-page app; the client library @microsoft/power-apps, which exposes connector APIs and the generated code; and the Power Apps host, which handles sign-in, loading and error messages. A file called power.config.json stores connection metadata for the CLI and library; you do not edit it in your logic.

Connections and connectors. Create a connection with pa connection create --connector <id> or find one with pa connection list. Then add it: pa app add data-source --connector shared_office365users --connection-id <id>. Tabular sources such as SQL or SharePoint also take --dataset and --table. The CLI writes typed files into src/generated/models and src/generated/services. Microsoft lists all connectors as supported except Excel Online (Business) and Excel Online (OneDrive).

Dataverse tables. Add a table with pa app add data-source --connector dataverse --table chd_ticket. The generated service has create, get, getAll, update and delete. getAll takes options: select, filter (OData), orderBy, top, skip, maxPageSize and skipToken for paging. Filter, sort and top are delegated to the server. You can read choice labels (formatted values) and set lookups with the Web API’s single-valued navigation property pattern. getMetadata returns table metadata such as columns and relationships.

Not supported for Dataverse today: polymorphic lookups, creating or changing table schema, FetchXML and alternate keys.

Dataverse actions and functions. Find one with pa app find-dataverse-api --search Escalate and add it with pa app add dataverse-api --api-name chd_EscalateTicket. The CLI reads the definition from $metadata and generates a service named after the operation. For a bound operation, the first argument is the ID of the row.

Cloud flows. Only solution-aware instant flows with the Power Apps trigger are supported. Use pa app list-flows, then pa app add flow --flow-id <id>. The generated service has a Run method that returns success, data and error. If the flow changes, run the add command again.

Copilot Studio agents. Add the connector shared_microsoftcopilotstudio as a data source. Call CopilotStudioService.ExecuteCopilotAsyncV2 with message, notificationUrl (a placeholder URL) and agentName, the published agent’s name from its Web app channel connection string. Read lastResponse or responses. Microsoft advises against ExecuteCopilot (it only returns a conversation ID) and ExecuteCopilotAsync (it can return 502 errors).

Environment variables and connection references. For ALM, bind a data source to a connection reference with --connection-ref and --solution-id. Tabular arguments such as a SharePoint site and list can point to environment variables with the @envvar: prefix and the variable’s schema name, so each environment uses its own values. pa app list-environment-variables lists what is available.

Context. getContext() from @microsoft/power-apps/app returns the app ID, environment ID, Dataverse URL, query parameters, and the user’s full name, object ID and UPN.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Goal: a React staff dashboard that lists open High priority tickets and can escalate one.

// Service names come from src/generated/services; check yours.
import { TicketService } from './generated/services/TicketService';
import { getContext } from '@microsoft/power-apps/app';

const ctx = await getContext();
const result = await TicketService.getAll({
  select: ['chd_title', 'chd_priority', 'chd_duedate'],
  filter: 'statecode eq 0',
  orderBy: ['chd_duedate asc'],
  top: 50
});
setTickets(result.data ?? []);
setGreeting('Hello ' + ctx.user.fullName);
  1. Initialize the app and add chd_ticket and chd_category as Dataverse data sources.
  2. Add Office 365 Users to show each staff member’s photo.
  3. Add the chd_EscalateTicket custom API with pa app add dataverse-api; an Escalate button passes the ticket ID.
  4. Add the solution-aware instant flow “Notify category owner” with pa app add flow and call its Run method after escalation.
  5. Add the Help Desk Assistant agent through the Copilot Studio connector so staff can ask “summarise today’s tickets”.
Watch out: code apps do not support Power Platform Git integration, are not available in Power Apps for Windows, and cannot be used as SharePoint forms.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to add a scheduled or automated flow. Only instant flows with the Power Apps trigger in a solution work.
  • Editing files in src/generated by hand. Refresh them with the CLI instead (pa app refresh data-source).
  • Sending read-only columns such as the primary key in create, or sending every column in update. Send only what changed.
  • Expecting FetchXML or alternate keys to work in a code app’s Dataverse source.
  • Binding to a personal connection when the app must move between environments. Use connection references.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Full control of the UI”, “React or Vue”, “VS Code”, “still governed by Power Platform” point to a code app.
  • “Call a custom API or Dataverse function from the code app” points to pa app add dataverse-api.
  • “Portable across Dev, Test and Prod” points to connection references and environment variables.
  • Answers that mention a scheduled flow, FetchXML or ExecuteCopilot for a reply are usually traps.

lessons.title: Deploy and manage code apps
lessons.summaryHtml:
After you build a code app you publish it with npm run build and pa app push. Then you manage it like any governed app.

  • ALM: push into a solution (preferred solution, or --solution-id), use connection references and environment variables, and deploy with Power Platform Pipelines. Git integration is not supported.
  • Sharing: share like a canvas app; pa app share grants play or edit. Users need a premium licence (or pay-as-you-go, App Pass or auto-claim).
  • Content Security Policy (CSP): set per environment in the admin center (Privacy + Security, App tab) or the Power Platform API. It is enforced by default and connect-src starts as 'none'.
  • Monitoring: send platform metrics to Application Insights through setConfig, and read health metrics in Monitor.
  • Troubleshooting: use browser DevTools; filter network calls by apihub.net (connectors) or dynamics.com (Dataverse) and read CSP errors in the Console.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Building a code app is like cooking a meal. Deploying and managing it is serving it in a restaurant: plating it (build), bringing it to the right table (publish into a solution and environment), deciding who may eat (sharing), following hygiene rules (Content Security Policy) and watching how guests react (monitoring). This lesson covers the restaurant side.

Why it matters

The Campus Help Desk staff dashboard works on your laptop. Now it must reach Test and Production, be shared with the right staff, call the Campus Directory API without being blocked, and warn you when it is slow. Admins also need to trust it. Code app assets are hosted on a publicly reachable endpoint and protected by Entra sign-in, so you must not bake secrets or sensitive data into the app itself. Keep data in sources that check the user first.

How it works

Build and publish. Run npm run build, then pa app push. The command returns a URL where the app runs, and the app appears in Power Apps.

Solutions and ALM. On the first publish, pa app push chooses a solution in this order: the environment’s preferred solution, then the Default solution, then no solution if the environment has no Dataverse. To choose one yourself, pass --solution-id (a GUID; names are not accepted). Later publishes keep the app in its solution. In a pipeline you can set PA_CLI_SOLUTION_ID. Once the app is in a solution, you deploy it with Power Platform Pipelines or solution export and import. Use connection references and environment variables so each stage uses its own connections and settings. Power Platform Git integration is not supported for code apps.

Publishing from CI/CD with a service principal.

  1. Once, a maker signs in and runs pa app share --principal <enterprise app object ID> --access edit. Environment permissions alone do not let the service principal update the app.
  2. In the pipeline, set PA_CLI_USE_SP_AUTH=true, SP_CLIENT_ID, SP_CLIENT_SECRET and SP_TENANT_ID.
  3. Run npm run build and pa app push --non-interactive. Exit code 0 means success.

Sharing and licensing. Code apps follow canvas app sharing limits. pa app share grants play (run) or edit (update) access. Users need a Power Apps Premium licence, or the environment uses pay-as-you-go, App Pass or auto-claim. Managed platform features apply: connector consent dialogs, DLP, Conditional Access per app, app quarantine, tenant isolation and health metrics. IP restrictions through SAS are not supported; use Conditional Access instead.

Content Security Policy. CSP tells the browser where the app may load scripts, images and data from. For code apps it is set per environment, in the admin center (environment settings, Product, Privacy + Security, Content security policy, App tab) or through the Power Platform API. For many environments, use environment groups and rules.

DirectiveDefault for code appsWhat it controls
connect-src'none'fetch and XHR calls to other sites
script-src'self' plus the platformWhere scripts load from
img-src'self' data: plus the platformImages
frame-ancestors'self' https://*.powerapps.comWho may embed the app in a frame
worker-src'none'Web workers

There are fifteen configurable directives. Values you add are appended to the default, except where the default is 'none'; then your values replace it. CSP is enforced by default. Enforce content security policy and Enable reporting are separate toggles, so you can collect violation reports at a reporting endpoint whether or not you enforce. Through the API the settings are PowerApps_CSPEnabledCodeApps, PowerApps_CSPReportingEndpoint and PowerApps_CSPConfigCodeApps.

Application Insights. The platform can hand you two metrics: sessionLoadSummary (did the app launch, time to interactive) and networkRequest (URL, method, duration, status, size). You forward them yourself:

import { ApplicationInsights } from '@microsoft/applicationinsights-web';
import { setConfig } from '@microsoft/power-apps/app';

const appInsights = new ApplicationInsights({ config: { connectionString: '<connection string>' } });
appInsights.loadAppInsights();

setConfig({
  logger: {
    logMetric: (value) => {
      appInsights.trackEvent({ name: value.type }, value.data);
    }
  }
});

Because connect-src blocks outside calls, add the Application Insights endpoints named in the Console’s CSP errors to connect-src. Changes can take a few minutes. Then query customEvents in KQL. Microsoft notes that environment variables are not supported for this key; keep it in a Dataverse settings table or pick it based on getContext().

Troubleshooting.

  • Browser DevTools (F12): in Network, filter by apihub.net for connector calls and dynamics.com for Dataverse calls, then read status codes and responses. In Console, read script errors and CSP violations.
  • Monitor in Power Apps shows app health for code apps: app open success rate, session count, time to interactive and time to full load. Data request success rate and latency are not shown for code apps, so use DevTools or Application Insights for those.
  • The header can be hidden for everyone with pa app set-setting --show-header false, or for one link with hideNavBar=true.

Performance. Watch time to interactive. Request only the columns you need with select, page large lists with top and maxPageSize, let filter and sort run on the server, and keep the production bundle small. The networkRequest metric shows which calls are slow.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Set Campus Help Desk as the preferred solution in Dev, then run npm run build and pa app push.
  2. Share the dashboard with the Help Desk Staff security group so it can run it.
  3. The dashboard calls the Campus Directory API with fetch and fails with a CSP error. Add the API’s domain to connect-src for the environment.
  4. Wire Application Insights with setConfig, add its endpoints to connect-src, and chart the 75th percentile of time to interactive per day.
  5. In Azure DevOps, a service principal that a maker shared the app with (edit) publishes each new build with pa app push --non-interactive; Pipelines then move the solution to Test and Production.
Remember: CSP is an environment setting, not something inside your app’s code. The same change affects every code app in that environment.

Common mistakes

  • Adding an outside domain to script-src when the failing call is a fetch. Network calls need connect-src.
  • Expecting environment permissions to let a service principal publish. A maker must share the app with it using edit access first.
  • Passing a solution name to --solution-id. It needs the GUID.
  • Putting keys or sensitive data in the app bundle, which is served from a public endpoint.
  • Relying on Monitor for data request latency in code apps. Use DevTools or Application Insights.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Violates the Content Security Policy directive” points to the environment’s code app CSP settings, usually connect-src.
  • “Non-interactive publishing from a pipeline” points to service principal variables, a one-time edit share and --non-interactive.
  • “Always land in the right solution” points to the preferred solution or --solution-id.
  • “Track load time and slow requests” points to Application Insights through setConfig and logMetric.

quiz.explanation: Filtering by dynamics.com isolates Dataverse requests; apihub.net isolates connector requests. The Console shows CSP and script errors.

domains.blurb: Plug-ins, custom APIs, platform APIs, Azure Functions, advanced flows and code-first agents.

lessons.title: Dataverse plug-ins
lessons.summaryHtml:
A plug-in is a .NET class that Dataverse runs on the server when a message, such as Create or Update, happens on a table. You register each plug-in as a step in the event execution pipeline: PreValidation (10), PreOperation (20) or PostOperation (40), synchronous or asynchronous.

  • The execution context tells the plug-in what happened: the message, the table, the Target row, the user, the depth and any images.
  • The Organization service, created from IOrganizationServiceFactory, lets the plug-in read and write other data.
  • You register with the Plug-in Registration Tool, trace with ITracingService, and can give a plug-in a managed identity to call Azure without secrets.

Plug-ins are for deterministic, server-side rules that must run no matter which app, flow or API changed the data.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A plug-in is a small piece of C# code that Dataverse runs on its own servers when something happens to data. “Something happens” is called a message: Create, Update, Delete, Assign and many more. You tell Dataverse which message, which table, and when in the process your code should run.

Think of an airport security line. Some checks happen before you even join the line (your ticket is checked). Some happen at the scanner (your bag is changed if needed). Some happen after you are through (a text message says your gate). Plug-ins can sit at each of these points.

Why it matters

Business rules and flows are great, but some logic must be guaranteed. If Priority must be High whenever a ticket mentions an outage, it must happen whether the ticket comes from the canvas app, the model-driven app, a flow, an import or the Web API. A synchronous plug-in runs inside Dataverse for every caller, and can even cancel the operation with a clear error. It is deterministic and fast, which is why the exam treats plug-ins as the main tool for server-side logic.

How it works

1. The event execution pipeline. Each message passes through numbered stages.

StageNumberIn the transaction?Typical use
PreValidation10No (may run outside it)Cancel early; checks before security checks and cascades
PreOperation20YesChange the Target values before they are saved
MainOperation30YesThe platform’s own work; only custom API plug-ins run here
PostOperation40Yes when synchronousWork that needs the saved row, such as its new ID

2. Synchronous vs asynchronous. A synchronous step runs while the user waits, and an exception rolls back the transaction. An asynchronous step is queued and run later by the asynchronous service; the user does not wait and a failure does not undo the save. Asynchronous steps are only allowed in PostOperation. Plug-ins run in a sandbox with a two-minute time limit, so long work belongs in Azure Functions.

3. The execution context. IPluginExecutionContext gives you MessageName, PrimaryEntityName, Stage, UserId, Depth, InputParameters, OutputParameters, the images and SharedVariables. For Create and Update, InputParameters["Target"] is an Entity. On Update it only contains the columns that changed. For Delete, Target is an EntityReference.

4. Images. A pre-image is a snapshot before the operation, a post-image a snapshot after it. You register them on the step with a name and only the columns you need. Pre-images do not exist on Create (there was no row) and post-images do not exist on Delete. Read them with context.PreEntityImages["PreImage"].

5. Depth and loops. If your plug-in updates a ticket and that update fires the same plug-in again, context.Depth goes up by one each time. The platform stops runaway chains at a maximum depth, but you should prevent loops yourself: use filtering attributes, change the Target in PreOperation instead of calling Update, and check depth only as a last guard.

6. Shared variables. context.SharedVariables passes values between plug-ins in the same pipeline, for example a PreOperation step that stores the old category for a PostOperation step. Do not use class fields for state: Dataverse caches plug-in instances, so they must be stateless and thread-safe.

7. The Organization service. Get IOrganizationServiceFactory from the service provider and call CreateOrganizationService(context.UserId) to act as the calling user (or null for the SYSTEM user). Every call costs time, so retrieve only needed columns and avoid calls when images already hold the data.

8. Tracing and errors. ITracingService.Trace writes to the Plug-in Trace Log when the environment setting is Exception or All. Throw InvalidPluginExecutionException with a friendly message to cancel a synchronous operation; the user sees that message.

9. Performance. Use filtering attributes on Update steps, keep synchronous code short, avoid ExecuteMultiple and parallel threads inside plug-ins, and move slow calls to asynchronous steps or Azure.

10. Registration. Create a project with pac plugin init. Register the signed assembly, or a plug-in package (a NuGet package that can carry dependent assemblies), with the Plug-in Registration Tool (pac tool prt). Then register steps and images, and add them to your solution. Set execution order when several steps share a stage.

11. Managed identity. To call Azure resources such as Key Vault without secrets, you create an app registration or user-assigned managed identity, sign the assembly or package with a certificate, add a federated identity credential in Azure, create a managedidentity record in Dataverse and link it to the assembly or package. In code, IManagedIdentityService.AcquireToken(scopes) returns a token.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Rule: when a ticket is created and its title or description mentions an urgent keyword, set Priority to High. Registered on Create of chd_ticket, PreOperation, synchronous.

public class SetPriorityFromKeywords : IPlugin
{
    private const int PriorityHigh = 100000002; // check your choice value
    public void Execute(IServiceProvider serviceProvider)
    {
        var context = (IPluginExecutionContext)serviceProvider.GetService(typeof(IPluginExecutionContext));
        var tracing = (ITracingService)serviceProvider.GetService(typeof(ITracingService));
        if (!context.InputParameters.Contains("Target")) return;
        var target = context.InputParameters["Target"] as Entity;
        if (target == null || target.LogicalName != "chd_ticket") return;

        string text = (target.GetAttributeValue<string>("chd_title") + " " +
            target.GetAttributeValue<string>("chd_description")).ToLowerInvariant();
        string[] urgent = { "outage", "exam", "fire", "cannot log in" };
        if (urgent.Any(k => text.Contains(k)))
        {
            target["chd_priority"] = new OptionSetValue(PriorityHigh);
            tracing.Trace("Priority set to High by keyword rule.");
        }
    }
}

No Update call is needed: in PreOperation, changing Target changes what is saved. For the Update step, register filtering attributes chd_title and chd_description and a pre-image, because Target only holds changed columns:

var pre = context.PreEntityImages.Contains("PreImage") ? context.PreEntityImages["PreImage"] : null;
string title = target.GetAttributeValue<string>("chd_title") ?? pre?.GetAttributeValue<string>("chd_title");
var factory = (IOrganizationServiceFactory)serviceProvider.GetService(typeof(IOrganizationServiceFactory));
var service = factory.CreateOrganizationService(context.UserId);
if (context.Depth > 1) return; // last-resort loop guard

A separate asynchronous PostOperation step could later notify the Campus Directory API, so students never wait for it.

Common mistakes

  • Calling service.Update on the same row in PreOperation. Just set the value on Target; the extra call wastes time and can cause loops.
  • Expecting all columns in Target on Update. Only changed columns are there; use a pre-image for the rest.
  • Registering an asynchronous step in PreOperation. Asynchronous is only allowed in PostOperation.
  • Storing data in class fields. Plug-in instances are cached and shared, so state leaks between calls.
  • Putting a long external call in a synchronous step. It slows every save and hits the two-minute limit.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Before it is saved”, “default a value”, “no extra update” point to PreOperation. “Cancel early”, “before security checks” point to PreValidation.
  • “Needs the new record ID” or “same transaction” point to synchronous PostOperation. “User must not wait” points to asynchronous.
  • “Old value”, “what changed” point to a pre-image. “Runs too often” points to filtering attributes.
  • “Pass a value between two plug-ins” points to SharedVariables. “No secrets, call Azure” points to managed identity.

A snapshot of column values before (pre-image) or after (post-image) the operation, registered on a step.
A counter in the context that goes up each time one operation triggers another; used to detect loops.
A property bag on the context that lets plug-ins in the same pipeline pass values to each other.
A Power Platform feature that lets a signed plug-in get Microsoft Entra tokens for Azure resources without storing secrets.
