lessons.title: Custom APIs and business events
lessons.summaryHtml:
A custom API creates your own Dataverse message, such as chd_EscalateTicket, with typed request parameters and response properties. Apps, flows, the Web API and the SDK call it like any built-in message.

  • You define it in the custom API table (unique name, binding, function or action, privacy, allowed step types) and add request parameters and response properties.
  • A plug-in class holds the main logic. You link it through the custom API’s Plugin Type, not by registering a step.
  • A business event is a custom API with no main plug-in, no response properties and “Async Only” steps. It is catalogued so subscribers, such as Power Automate, can react to it.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dataverse ships with many messages: Create, Update, Assign, QualifyLead and so on. A custom API lets you add your own message with your own name, inputs and outputs. Once it exists, every client can call it: the Web API, the SDK, cloud flows, canvas apps (through the Dataverse connector’s unbound or bound action) and client scripts.

Think of a restaurant menu. Built-in messages are the standard dishes. A custom API is a new dish you add to the menu, with a clear name and a list of ingredients (parameters) and what comes out of the kitchen (response). Customers order it the same way as any other dish.

A business event is the opposite direction. Instead of someone asking for work, Dataverse announces “this just happened”, and anyone who subscribed hears about it.

Why it matters

Without custom APIs, teams copy the same logic into flows, apps and scripts. When the rule changes, one copy is forgotten. A custom API puts the logic in one place on the server, with typed parameters and its own security privilege. Business events solve the integration side: other systems can react to meaningful moments (a ticket was escalated) instead of watching every row update and guessing.

How it works

1. The custom API row. Custom APIs are data in three tables: customapi, customapirequestparameter and customapiresponseproperty. You create them in the maker portal (inside a solution), with code, or in the Plug-in Registration Tool.

PropertyWhat it controls
Unique nameThe message name, with your publisher prefix, such as chd_EscalateTicket
Binding typeGlobal, Entity (one row) or EntityCollection
Bound entity logical nameThe table when bound, such as chd_ticket
Is functionYes: called with GET, must not change data. No: an action called with POST
Is privateHides it from the metadata document; it still works for those who know it
Allowed custom processing step typeNone, Async Only, or Sync and Async steps by others
Execute privilege nameOptional privilege a caller must hold to run it
Plugin TypeThe plug-in class that does the main work

2. Parameters and properties. Request parameters and response properties have a unique name, a type (for example Boolean, DateTime, Decimal, Entity, EntityReference, Integer, Money, Picklist, String, Guid) and an optional flag. Types are enforced, so callers get a clear error when they send the wrong thing.

3. The main plug-in. The plug-in is an ordinary IPlugin. It reads context.InputParameters and writes context.OutputParameters. For a bound API, InputParameters["Target"] is an EntityReference to the row. You connect the class through the Plugin Type column; it runs in the main operation stage. You do not register a step for it.

4. Calling it. Bound actions use the table’s entity set name and the Microsoft.Dynamics.CRM namespace. Global actions are called at the root. In the SDK you use new OrganizationRequest("chd_EscalateTicket") and set parameters.

5. Business events. To define a custom business event you create a custom API with Allowed custom processing step type = Async Only, no Plugin Type and no response properties, only request parameters. Then you add it to a catalog (Catalog and CatalogAssignment tables) under a category. Subscribers include Power Automate’s Dataverse trigger When an action is performed, Azure Service Bus, Azure Event Hubs, webhooks and asynchronous plug-in steps. Standard table events (Create, Update, Delete) use the separate “When a row is added, modified or deleted” trigger.

Remember: keep business events specific and lightweight. They say that something happened; they are not a data export channel.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Staff often escalate tickets. You define chd_EscalateTicket: binding Entity on chd_ticket, action, request parameter chd_Reason (String), response property chd_NewPriority (Integer).

public void Execute(IServiceProvider serviceProvider)
{
    var context = (IPluginExecutionContext)serviceProvider.GetService(typeof(IPluginExecutionContext));
    var factory = (IOrganizationServiceFactory)serviceProvider.GetService(typeof(IOrganizationServiceFactory));
    var service = factory.CreateOrganizationService(context.UserId);

    const int PriorityHigh = 100000002; // your High choice value
    var ticketRef = (EntityReference)context.InputParameters["Target"];
    var reason = (string)context.InputParameters["chd_Reason"];
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(reason))
        throw new InvalidPluginExecutionException("Please give a reason for escalation.");

    var update = new Entity("chd_ticket", ticketRef.Id);
    update["chd_priority"] = new OptionSetValue(PriorityHigh);
    update["chd_escalationreason"] = reason;
    service.Update(update);
    context.OutputParameters["chd_NewPriority"] = PriorityHigh;
}

Calling it with the Web API:

POST /api/data/v9.2/chd_tickets(00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001)/Microsoft.Dynamics.CRM.chd_EscalateTicket
Content-Type: application/json

{ "chd_Reason": "Exam starts in one hour" }

A command button in Help Desk Staff can call the same message with Xrm.WebApi.online.execute, and a cloud flow can call it with the Dataverse action “Perform a bound action”. The logic exists once.

Next, a business event chd_TicketResolved (Global, Async Only, request parameter chd_TicketId, no plug-in, no response) is added to a “Help Desk events” catalog. When a ticket is closed, the escalation plug-in (or a flow) calls the message. A Power Automate flow with “When an action is performed” sends a satisfaction survey, and a Service Bus endpoint feeds the campus reporting system.

Common mistakes

  • Registering a step for the main custom API plug-in. Use the Plugin Type column instead.
  • Making a function that changes data. Functions are for reads and are called with GET.
  • Adding response properties to a business event. Events announce; they do not answer.
  • Forgetting the publisher prefix, or creating the API outside a solution, which breaks ALM.
  • Using Sync and Async when you do not want others slowing your message. Choose None or Async Only.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Reusable operation called from apps, flows and code”, “typed inputs and outputs” point to a custom API.
  • “Read only”, “GET” point to Is function = Yes. “Operates on one record” points to Entity binding.
  • “Prevent others from adding synchronous logic” points to Async Only or None.
  • “Notify subscribers”, “When an action is performed”, “catalog” point to business events.

Whether the API is Global, bound to one row of a table (Entity) or bound to a collection of rows (EntityCollection).
A function (IsFunction = true) is called with GET and must not change data; an action is called with POST.
Controls which extra steps others may register on your message: None, Async Only, or Sync and Async.
A message raised when something meaningful happens, catalogued so flows, webhooks, Service Bus or Event Hub can subscribe.
Tables (Catalog and CatalogAssignment) that group business events into categories so they appear to subscribers.

lessons.title: Platform APIs and the SDKs
lessons.summaryHtml:
Code outside Dataverse talks to it through two doors: the Web API (REST and OData at /api/data/v9.2/, any language) and the Organization service used by the SDK for .NET. A newer Dataverse SDK for Python wraps the Web API for Python users.

  • Every caller authenticates with OAuth tokens from Microsoft Entra ID, usually through MSAL.
  • For volume, use CreateMultiple and UpdateMultiple. ExecuteMultiple batches different requests; ExecuteTransaction makes them all-or-nothing.
  • Service protection limits return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After value. Good clients wait and retry.
  • Background operations run a custom API asynchronously and let you poll or receive a callback.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dataverse is a database behind a web service. External code cannot open the database directly; it must go through the APIs. There are two main doors. The Web API is a REST service that speaks JSON and OData, so any language can use it. The Organization service is what the SDK for .NET uses, with typed classes such as Entity and QueryExpression. Both run the same pipeline, so plug-ins, security and auditing apply either way.

Think of a bank. You can use the counter (Web API, anyone can walk up) or the bank’s own app (SDK, easier if you use its platform). The vault rules are the same.

Why it matters

Integrations move data in volume: nightly imports, reporting jobs, data science notebooks. A careless client sends one request per row, ignores throttling and fails halfway. A good client picks the right API, uses bulk messages, respects service protection limits, handles concurrency and authenticates securely with OAuth. The exam tests these choices.

How it works

1. Web API and OData queries. The endpoint is https://yourorg.crm.dynamics.com/api/data/v9.2/. Tables are addressed by their entity set name (chd_tickets). Query options:

  • $select picks columns (always use it). $filter filters with eq, ne, gt, lt, and, or, and functions such as contains and startswith.
  • $orderby, $top, $expand (related rows), $apply (grouping and aggregation) and $count.
  • Lookups appear as _chd_category_value. Paging uses the Prefer: odata.maxpagesize header and @odata.nextLink.
  • Prefer: odata.include-annotations="OData.Community.Display.V1.FormattedValue" returns choice labels and formatted dates. You can also send FetchXML with ?fetchXml=.

2. Organization service. IOrganizationService has Create, Retrieve, RetrieveMultiple, Update, Delete, Associate, Disassociate and Execute. For modern .NET use ServiceClient from Microsoft.PowerPlatform.Dataverse.Client. It has async methods and built-in retry for service protection errors.

3. Bulk and batching.

OptionWhat it doesTransaction
CreateMultiple / UpdateMultiple / UpsertMultipleMany rows of one table in one request; best throughputYes for standard tables: one failure fails the request
ExecuteMultipleUp to 1,000 mixed requests; ContinueOnError and ReturnResponses settingsNo, each request is separate
ExecuteTransactionMixed requests that must succeed or fail togetherYes, all or nothing
Web API $batchSeveral HTTP requests in one call; a change set is a transactionOnly inside a change set

Plug-ins registered on Create or Update also run for CreateMultiple and UpdateMultiple, because the pipelines are merged. Do not use ExecuteMultiple or ExecuteTransaction inside plug-ins.

4. Concurrency. Two users can overwrite each other. Use optimistic concurrency: send If-Match with the row’s @odata.etag; if the row changed, you get 412 Precondition Failed. In the SDK, set ConcurrencyBehavior.IfRowVersionMatches with the RowVersion.

5. Service protection limits. They are evaluated per user over a sliding 5-minute window: by default 6,000 requests, 20 minutes of combined execution time, and 52 concurrent requests. When exceeded, the Web API returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header in seconds. The SDK throws a fault whose ErrorDetails contains a Retry-After TimeSpan. Microsoft recommends parallel single or bulk requests with a sensible degree of parallelism, and waiting as told.

catch (FaultException<OrganizationServiceFault> ex)
    when (ex.Detail.ErrorDetails.ContainsKey("Retry-After"))
{
    var wait = (TimeSpan)ex.Detail.ErrorDetails["Retry-After"];
    await Task.Delay(wait);   // then retry the same request
}

6. OAuth with MSAL. Every call carries Authorization: Bearer with an Entra ID token whose scope is your environment URL plus /.default. Interactive apps use a public client and sign the user in. Services use a confidential client (client credentials flow) with a certificate or secret, and the app must exist in Dataverse as an application user with a security role.

var app = ConfidentialClientApplicationBuilder.Create(clientId)
    .WithClientSecret(secret)
    .WithAuthority("https://login.microsoftonline.com/" + tenantId)
    .Build();
var token = await app.AcquireTokenForClient(
    new[] { "https://yourorg.crm.dynamics.com/.default" }).ExecuteAsync();

7. Background operations. The ExecuteBackgroundOperation message runs a custom API asynchronously, so the client does not hold a connection open. It returns a BackgroundOperationId and a Location URL. You can poll the backgroundoperation table or that status URL, pass a CallbackUri to be notified, or register a step on OnBackgroundOperationComplete. The custom API plug-in still has the two-minute limit, and the feature is marked preview on Microsoft Learn at the time of writing.

8. Dataverse SDK for Python. The package PowerPlatform-Dataverse-Client gives Python developers create, retrieve, update, delete, bulk operations and a query builder that can return pandas DataFrames. It authenticates with azure.identity credentials.

from azure.identity import InteractiveBrowserCredential
from PowerPlatform.Dataverse.client import DataverseClient

client = DataverseClient(base_url="https://yourorg.crm.dynamics.com",
                         credential=InteractiveBrowserCredential())
ticket_id = client.records.create("chd_ticket", {"chd_title": "Projector broken"})
ticket = client.records.retrieve("chd_ticket", ticket_id)

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The staff dashboard needs open High-priority tickets with their category name: 
    GET /api/data/v9.2/chd_tickets?$select=chd_title,chd_duedate
  &$filter=chd_status ne [Closed value] and chd_priority eq [High value]
  &$expand=chd_Category($select=chd_name)&$orderby=chd_duedate asc&$top=50
    (The expand uses the lookup’s navigation property name, which you can see in the metadata.)
  2. At term start, 30,000 tickets are migrated from an old system. A .NET job with an application user sends CreateMultipleRequest batches of Entity objects in parallel and handles Retry-After.
  3. When a ticket is merged, the job closes the duplicate and moves its notes. These mixed requests go in one ExecuteTransactionRequest so nothing is half done.
  4. Two staff edit the same ticket. The dashboard sends If-Match with the etag, catches 412 and asks the user to reload.
  5. The data team analyses ticket trends in a Jupyter notebook with the Python SDK and pandas.

Common mistakes

  • Omitting $select or ColumnSet(true). Fetching every column is slow.
  • Treating ExecuteMultiple as a transaction. It is not; use ExecuteTransaction or a change set.
  • Retrying 429 errors immediately. Always honour Retry-After.
  • Using a user’s password in a service. Use client credentials and an application user.
  • Expecting ExecuteMultiple to be faster than bulk messages for one table. CreateMultiple and UpdateMultiple are built for that.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Many rows, same table, best performance” points to CreateMultiple/UpdateMultiple. “All or nothing” points to ExecuteTransaction or a change set.
  • “429”, “throttled” point to Retry-After. “Lost update” points to If-Match / RowVersion.
  • “No user present”, “daemon” point to client credentials + application user.
  • “Do not keep the connection open”, “long custom API” point to background operations. “Python, pandas” points to the Python SDK.

terms.definition: The REST query standard used by the Web API: $select, $filter, $orderby, $top, $expand and more.
The SDK interface (IOrganizationService) with Create, Retrieve, RetrieveMultiple, Update, Delete, Associate, Disassociate and Execute.
Bulk messages that create or update many rows of one table in one request, faster than many single calls.
Runs a set of requests in one database transaction; if one fails, all are rolled back.
Per-user limits on number of requests, execution time and concurrent requests; exceeding them returns 429 with Retry-After.
Microsoft Authentication Library, used to get Entra ID access tokens for Dataverse.

lessons.examTip: “All or nothing” means ExecuteTransaction (or a $batch change set). “Thousands of rows, same table” means CreateMultiple/UpdateMultiple. “429” means read Retry-After and wait.

quiz.question: A nightly import creates 50,000 tickets. Performance matters and all rows are in the same table. What should the .NET code use?
options: One Create call per row in a loop
CreateMultiple with batches of rows, several batches in parallel
A $batch with one change set per row
quiz.explanation: CreateMultiple is optimised for many rows of one table. Parallel batches use the server capacity within service protection limits.

quiz.question: Your integration gets HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from the Web API. What should it do?
options: Read the Retry-After header, wait that long, then retry
Retry immediately in a tight loop
Switch to another user account for every call
quiz.explanation: Service protection errors include Retry-After. Waiting that long and retrying is the documented approach.

quiz.question: Creating a ticket and its two related task rows must succeed or fail together. The requests are of different types. What should you use with the SDK?
quiz.explanation: ExecuteTransaction runs mixed requests in one transaction and rolls back everything if one fails.

quiz.question: A daemon service with no signed-in user must call Dataverse. How should it authenticate?
options: MSAL public client with username and password
An Entra app registration with a certificate or secret, registered as an application user, using the client credentials flow
An API key in the request header
quiz.explanation: Server-to-server calls use a confidential client (client credentials) and an application user with a security role in Dataverse.

lessons.title: Azure Functions for Power Platform
lessons.summaryHtml:
Azure Functions run your code in Azure on demand. In Power Platform solutions they take the work that plug-ins should not do: long-running jobs, scheduled jobs and event-driven processing of messages sent from Dataverse.

  • Triggers start a function: Timer (a schedule), HTTP, Azure Service Bus, Azure Event Hubs and more.
  • Durable Functions coordinate long, multi-step work with checkpoints.
  • A managed identity lets the function get tokens for Dataverse without secrets. You add it to the environment as an application user with a security role.

Functions can also sit behind a custom connector so apps and flows can call them.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Azure Functions is a serverless service: you write a function, and Azure runs it when something triggers it. You do not manage servers. You pay mainly for what runs (depending on the hosting plan).

If a plug-in is a staff member who must answer within two minutes while the student waits at the counter, an Azure Function is the back office. It can work at night, take its time, and pick up jobs from an inbox when it is ready.

Why it matters

Plug-ins run in a sandbox with a two-minute limit and must react to a Dataverse message. Cloud flows are great for low-code automation but are harder to test and version as code, and complex loops over thousands of rows can be slow. Azure Functions fill the gap for long-running work, scheduled work and event-driven integration, with full C#, Python or JavaScript, unit tests and Application Insights monitoring.

How it works

1. Triggers and bindings. A trigger starts the function. Bindings connect inputs and outputs without boilerplate.

TriggerStarts whenPower Platform use
TimerAn NCRONTAB schedule firesNightly SLA checks, clean-up jobs
HTTPA request arrivesWebhook target, backend for a custom connector
Azure Service BusA queue or topic message arrivesReliable processing of Dataverse events
Azure Event HubsEvents stream inHigh-volume event streams

The Timer schedule has six fields: second, minute, hour, day, month, day of week. 0 0 2 * * * means 02:00:00 every day. The default time zone is UTC.

2. Long-running work. Hosting plans have different time limits; the classic Consumption plan has a short maximum run time, while other plans allow longer runs. For work that must span a long time or many steps, use Durable Functions: an orchestrator calls activity functions, and state is checkpointed so work survives restarts. Also design for idempotency: if a message is processed twice, the result should be the same.

3. Event-driven integration from Dataverse. With the Plug-in Registration Tool you register a service endpoint (Service Bus queue or topic, Event Hub, or webhook) and then a step on it, such as Update of chd_ticket, asynchronous. Dataverse posts the execution context (in a message format you choose, such as JSON). A Service Bus-triggered function reads it. Queues keep messages if the function is down, which makes this more reliable than a direct webhook.

4. Managed identity to Dataverse. Turn on a system-assigned (tied to the Function App) or user-assigned (a separate reusable resource) managed identity. In the Power Platform admin center, create an application user with that identity’s application (client) ID and give it a least-privilege security role. In code, DefaultAzureCredential or ManagedIdentityCredential from Azure.Identity gets a token for the environment URL plus /.default. No secret is stored anywhere.

5. Calling back into Power Platform. Use ServiceClient with a token provider function, or plain HttpClient with the Web API. Respect service protection limits and Retry-After, and use bulk messages for volume.

6. Monitoring and configuration. Connect Application Insights for logs, failures and performance. Keep the environment URL and other settings in app settings (or Key Vault), so the same code runs against dev, test and production.

Watch out: a managed identity alone gives no access to Dataverse. Without an application user and a security role, calls fail with an authorization error.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Requirement: every night, find open tickets past their Due date, raise their priority and log an escalation. The job may touch thousands of rows.

public class NightlySlaCheck
{
    [Function("NightlySlaCheck")]
    public async Task Run([TimerTrigger("0 0 2 * * *")] TimerInfo timer)
    {
        string url = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("DataverseUrl");
        var credential = new DefaultAzureCredential();
        using var svc = new ServiceClient(new Uri(url), async _ =>
            (await credential.GetTokenAsync(
                new TokenRequestContext(new[] { url + "/.default" }))).Token);

        var query = new QueryExpression("chd_ticket") { ColumnSet = new ColumnSet("chd_title") };
        query.Criteria.AddCondition("chd_duedate", ConditionOperator.LessThan, DateTime.UtcNow);
        query.Criteria.AddCondition("chd_status", ConditionOperator.NotEqual, StatusClosed);
        EntityCollection overdue = await svc.RetrieveMultipleAsync(query);
        // build Entity updates and send them with UpdateMultiple in batches
    }
}
  1. The Function App has a system-assigned managed identity, added as application user “SLA Checker” with a role that can read and update chd_ticket.
  2. Updates go out with UpdateMultiple in batches. The escalation itself can reuse the chd_EscalateTicket custom API so the rule lives in one place.
  3. A second function, triggered by Service Bus, receives ticket updates from a Dataverse service endpoint and syncs them to the campus reporting system.
  4. An HTTP-triggered function, secured with Entra ID, becomes the backend of the “Campus Directory API” custom connector used by the canvas app.

Common mistakes

  • Putting long jobs in plug-ins. The two-minute sandbox limit and user wait time make this fail.
  • Enabling managed identity but forgetting the application user and security role in Dataverse.
  • Reading the Timer schedule as five-field cron. Azure Functions NCRONTAB starts with seconds.
  • Using a direct webhook when the receiver may be down. Use Service Bus for guaranteed delivery.
  • Writing non-idempotent handlers. Retries and duplicate messages then create duplicate data.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Every night”, “on a schedule” point to a Timer trigger. “Longer than two minutes”, “many steps with state” point to Durable Functions.
  • “No credentials in code”, “no secrets” point to a managed identity + application user.
  • “Must not lose events”, “consumer may be offline” point to a Service Bus endpoint with a Service Bus trigger.
  • “Custom logic behind a connector” points to an HTTP-triggered function used by a custom connector.

terms.definition: The event that starts a function, such as a timer schedule, an HTTP request or a new Service Bus message.
The six-field schedule format of the Timer trigger: second, minute, hour, day, month, day of week.
An extension for long-running, stateful workflows made of orchestrator and activity functions.
An identity in Microsoft Entra ID that Azure manages for a resource, so code gets tokens without stored secrets.
A non-interactive Dataverse user linked to an Entra app or managed identity, with security roles like any user.
A Dataverse registration that posts the execution context to Service Bus, Event Hubs or a webhook.

lessons.examTip: “Runs longer than a plug-in allows” or “every night” means Azure Function. “No secrets” means managed identity plus an application user.

steps: Download the exercise files into a folder named NightlySlaCheck and open it in VS Code with the Azure Functions extension installed.
Copy local.settings.sample.json to local.settings.json and set DataverseUrl to your environment URL. Keep DryRun set to true.
Start Azurite (the local storage emulator), sign in with az login using your developer account, and start the project with F5 or func start.
Run the timer function now instead of waiting for 02:00 UTC: send POST http://localhost:7071/admin/functions/NightlySlaCheck with Content-Type application/json and the body {}, then read the log.
Create a Function App (.NET 8, isolated worker) in Azure, deploy the project and add the app settings DataverseUrl, PriorityHighValue, StatusClosedValue and DryRun (true).

Turn on the system-assigned managed identity. Copy its application (client) ID from Microsoft Entra ID > Enterprise applications and add an application user for it in the Power Platform admin center with a role that can read and update chd_ticket.

Run the function from the portal (Test/Run) and check the traces in Application Insights. Keep DryRun true so the shared ticket data stays as in tickets.csv; set it to false only in an environment you can reset.
check: The project builds, and the local run logs “Found 12 overdue tickets, 11 need escalation.” (with the 28 rows of tickets.csv, run after 3 September 2026).
The log lists 12 “Overdue:” lines and ends with “DryRun is true: no rows were updated.”; no ticket Priority changes.
Before the application user exists, the Azure run fails with “Dataverse connection failed”; after you add it, the same run logs “Found 12 overdue tickets”.
Application Insights shows the “Found 12 overdue tickets, 11 need escalation.” trace for the portal run.

quiz.question: Every night at 02:00, overdue tickets must be checked and escalated. The job can take 20 minutes. Where should the logic run?
options: A client script on form load
A Timer-triggered Azure Function (using Durable Functions or a plan that allows long runs)
quiz.explanation: Plug-ins have a two-minute limit and need an event. A timer-triggered function runs on a schedule and can be designed for long work.

quiz.question: Your Azure Function must call Dataverse. Security forbids storing secrets. What must you configure besides enabling the managed identity?
options: An application user in the environment for the identity, with a security role
A client secret in app settings
quiz.explanation: Dataverse only trusts identities that exist as users. The managed identity becomes an application user and gets its access from security roles.

quiz.question: Ticket updates must be processed by Azure code reliably even if the code is down for an hour. Which pattern fits best?
options: A webhook that calls the function directly
A cloud flow with a 1-hour delay
A plug-in that calls the function with HttpClient
A Service Bus service endpoint on the step, with a Service Bus-triggered function
quiz.explanation: Service Bus queues keep messages until the consumer is ready, so processing survives downtime.

quiz.question: A Timer trigger uses 0 30 6 * * 1-5. When does it run?
options: At 06:30 on the first five days of every month
At 30 seconds past 6 minutes every hour
quiz.explanation: NCRONTAB has six fields: second, minute, hour, day, month, day of week. 1-5 is Monday to Friday.

lessons.title: Advanced cloud flows and Copilot Studio workflows
lessons.summaryHtml:
As a developer you write flows that behave well when things go wrong. You combine expressions to shape data, use scopes and Configure run after to build try, catch and finally blocks, and add trigger conditions so a flow only runs when it should.

  • Retry policies decide how an action repeats after a temporary failure.
  • Child flows let one solution-aware flow call another, so shared logic lives in one place.
  • The Dataverse connector can sign in as a service principal (an app registration), so the flow does not depend on one person’s account.
  • Agent flows built in Copilot Studio start with When an agent calls the flow and return data with Respond to the agent.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In AB-410 and PL-900 you built flows that work on a sunny day. As a developer you build flows that also survive a rainy day. That means clear data handling with expressions, careful error handling, smart triggers that do not start when they are not needed, and reusable pieces such as child flows.

Think of a railway. A beginner lays a track from A to B. An engineer also adds signals (trigger conditions), sidings for broken trains (catch blocks), repair crews that try again (retry policies) and shared stations that many lines use (child flows).

Copilot Studio adds agent flows. These are deterministic flows, built with the same designer, that an agent calls as a tool. They start with When an agent calls the flow and return values with Respond to the agent.

Why it matters

A flow that fails silently is worse than no flow. If the Campus Help Desk escalation flow stops working, High priority tickets sit unseen. Staff think the system is fine because nothing complains.

Good flows also save capacity. Every run counts against request limits. A flow that starts on every ticket update, then ends at a Condition, wastes runs. The exam expects you to choose the option that prevents the run, not the one that exits early.

How it works

1. Complex expressions. Expressions are functions inside @{ } or in the expression editor. You combine them.

@{formatDateTime(addDays(utcNow(), 2), 'yyyy-MM-dd')}
@{coalesce(triggerOutputs()?['body/chd_description'], 'No description')}
@{if(equals(outputs('Get_category')?['body/chd_name'], 'Network'), 'IT team', 'Front desk')}

The ? operator returns null instead of failing when a property is missing. Filter array and Select reshape arrays without a loop. join and split turn arrays into text and back.

2. Flow control and error handling. A scope groups actions. The scope fails if any action inside fails. Configure run after decides when the next action runs: is successful, has failed, is skipped or has timed out. Together they form a pattern:

ScopeRun after settingPurpose
TryDefault (previous succeeded)The normal work
CatchTry has failed or has timed outLog the error, alert someone
FinallyCatch succeeded, failed or skippedClean-up that always runs

Inside Catch, result('Try') returns the status and outputs of each action in the Try scope. Filter it to find the failed action and its error message. End Catch with Terminate set to Failed. Otherwise the run shows as Succeeded, because the Catch scope itself succeeded.

3. Trigger filtering. The Dataverse trigger has Change type, Table name, Scope, Select columns (start only when these columns change) and Filter rows (an OData filter). In trigger settings you can also add trigger conditions: expressions that must all be true. If a condition is false, the flow does not run at all.

@equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/chd_priority'], 100000002)

Choice columns store numbers, not labels. Check the real value of High in your column before writing the condition.

4. Retry policies. HTTP-based actions have a retry policy in their settings. Options are Default, None, Exponential interval and Fixed interval. You set a count and an interval written in ISO 8601 format, such as PT30S for thirty seconds. Retries help with temporary errors such as throttling. They do not fix a wrong row ID.

5. Child flows. A parent flow calls a child with Run a child flow. The child starts with Manually trigger a flow and returns values with Respond to a PowerApp or flow. Both flows must be in a solution. The child should use its own embedded connections rather than asking run-only users for theirs.

6. Service principal for Dataverse. The Dataverse connector can connect with a service principal. You register an app in Microsoft Entra ID, create a secret or certificate, add an application user in the environment and give it a security role. The flow then runs as that app, not as a person.

7. Agent flows. In Copilot Studio an agent can call a flow as a tool. The flow must respond within the action time limit, so keep queries small. For longer work, the Respond to the agent action has an asynchronous response option.

Watch out: a Condition as the first action still counts as a run. To avoid the run, filter at the trigger.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Create the flow Escalate High Tickets in the Campus Help Desk solution. Trigger: Dataverse, Added or Modified, Tickets, Select columns chd_priority.
  2. Add the trigger condition for High. Now edits to Title or Description never start the flow.
  3. Scope Try: Get a row by ID for the Category, then Run a child flow Calculate SLA, passing the priority and created on date. The child returns a due date built with addDays.
  4. Still in Try: update the ticket’s Due date and post to the staff Teams channel.
  5. Scope Catch (run after Try has failed or has timed out): a Filter array on result('Try') where status equals Failed, a Compose with the error message, an email to the flow owner with a link built from workflow()?['run']?['name'], then Terminate with status Failed.
  6. Switch the Dataverse connection references to a service principal connection. The flow keeps running when staff change.
  7. In Copilot Studio, build an agent flow Get Ticket Status that Help Desk Assistant calls with a ticket number and that returns status and due date through Respond to the agent.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting Terminate in Catch, so failed runs look successful in run history.
  • Writing trigger conditions against the choice label (“High”) instead of the stored number.
  • Using a Condition after the trigger to exit early and thinking it saves runs.
  • Building child flows outside a solution; Run a child flow only lists flows in the same solution.
  • Expecting retries to fix logic errors. Retries only help with temporary faults.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Only when a column changes” or “reduce runs” → Select columns, Filter rows or a trigger condition.
  • “Handle failures of several actions together” or “notify on any failure” → scopes with Configure run after, often with result().
  • “Reuse logic across flows” → a solution-aware child flow.
  • “Flow must not depend on a user account” → service principal connection with an application user.

terms.definition: An action that groups other actions so they succeed or fail together, used to build try and catch blocks.
Setting that makes an action run only when the previous action succeeded, failed, was skipped or timed out.
An expression on the trigger that must be true, or the flow does not start at all.
Action setting that controls whether and how often a failed request is retried.
A solution-aware flow started by another flow with Run a child flow, returning values with a response action.
An app identity from a Microsoft Entra app registration, used instead of a person’s account.

lessons.examTip: “Run only when Priority is High, without wasting runs” points to a trigger condition or Filter rows. “Handle any failure in a group of actions” points to a scope plus Configure run after.

steps: Download the exercise files. Open flow-expressions.txt from the start folder and sample-flow-data.json, and write your answers to E1 to E10 before you build anything.

In make.powerautomate.com open Solutions > Campus Help Desk and create an automated cloud flow Escalate High Tickets with the Dataverse trigger When a row is added, modified or deleted: Added or Modified, table Tickets, Select columns chd_priority.
In the trigger settings add your E2 expression as a trigger condition, using the Priority and Status values stored in your environment.

Add a scope named Try with Get a row by ID (table Categories, row ID from the ticket’s category lookup) and a Teams post whose message uses your E6 expression. Set the Teams action’s retry policy from E10.

Add a scope named Catch, set Configure run after to has failed and has timed out only, and inside it add Filter array (E7), a Compose with E8, a Compose with E9 and a Terminate action with status Failed.

Create a child flow Calculate SLA in the solution with Manually trigger a flow (inputs Priority and Created on), Composes for E3 and E4 using those inputs, and Respond to a PowerApp or flow returning DueDate. Call it from Try with Run a child flow.
Change the Dataverse connection reference to a connection that uses a service principal (client ID, secret, tenant) for your application user from lesson D.11.
Test: set CHD-1025 to High, then change only its Title. Next, put 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 as the row ID in Get a row by ID and set CHD-1025 to High again.
Compare your answers with flow-expressions.txt in the solution folder, then set CHD-1025 back to Priority Medium and restore the row ID.
check: Your answers match the solution: E1 and E2 return true, E3 returns 1, E4 returns 2026-08-29 and E7 keeps 1 item (Get_a_row_by_ID).
Setting CHD-1025 to High starts exactly one run; changing only its Title starts none.
With the empty row ID the run shows Failed in run history, the Catch scope ran, and the E8 Compose output ends with “Does Not Exist”.
The Calculate SLA child run returns a due date one day after the ticket’s Created on value (High = 1 day).

quiz.question: A flow on Ticket updates runs thousands of times a day, but it only needs to act when Priority changes to High. What reduces unnecessary runs most?
options: Add a Condition as the first action
Set Select columns to chd_priority and add a trigger condition for High
Add a Delay of one minute
quiz.explanation: Select columns limits the trigger to changes in Priority, and a trigger condition stops the run from starting unless Priority is High. A Condition action still counts a run.

quiz.question: You wrap four actions in a scope named Try. A second scope, Catch, must run only when something inside Try fails or times out. What do you configure?
options: A trigger condition on the flow
Configure run after on Catch: has failed and has timed out
quiz.explanation: Configure run after on the Catch scope, pointing at Try, with has failed and has timed out selected, creates the catch behaviour.

quiz.question: A nightly flow uses the Dataverse connector with a staff member’s account. The account is disabled when the person leaves and the flow breaks. What is the best fix?
options: Use a Dataverse connection that authenticates with a service principal mapped to an application user
Share the flow with a second owner
Convert the flow to a desktop flow
quiz.explanation: A service principal connection uses an app registration and an application user with a security role, so it does not depend on a person’s account.

quiz.question: Three flows repeat the same ten-step SLA calculation. You want one copy of the logic that returns a due date. What should you build?
options: A copy of the actions in each flow
A scheduled flow that writes to a table
A solution-aware child flow called with Run a child flow
quiz.explanation: A child flow in the same solution holds the shared logic and returns values to the parent through a response action.

lessons.title: Code-first agents with Microsoft Foundry
lessons.summaryHtml:
Microsoft Foundry is the Azure platform where developers build agents in code. A Foundry agent can reach Power Platform through MCP servers: for example the Dataverse MCP server exposes tools such as search_data, read_query and create_record.

  • Copilot Studio agents can connect to other agents, including Foundry agents (preview), agents over the A2A protocol and other Copilot Studio agents.
  • Work IQ (preview) grounds agents in work context such as mail, meetings, files and business systems; its MCP servers include one for Dataverse and Dynamics 365. It runs on behalf of the signed-in user.
  • The Copilot Studio client library in the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK lets your own app or code talk to a published Copilot Studio agent.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Copilot Studio is where makers build agents with low code. Microsoft Foundry is where developers build agents with code. In Foundry you choose the model, write instructions, add tools and control orchestration from Python, C# or other SDKs. The two worlds connect: Foundry agents can use Power Platform data, and Copilot Studio agents can call Foundry agents.

Picture a hospital. Copilot Studio is the reception team: friendly, fast and trained with checklists. Foundry is the specialist lab: custom equipment and full control. Patients (users) arrive at reception, which sends hard cases to the lab and gets answers back.

This lesson covers four links between the two worlds: MCP servers, connected agents, Work IQ and the Copilot Studio client library. Several of these features are in preview. Describe them by purpose, and check current docs before relying on detail.

Why it matters

Organisations rarely have one kind of agent. The data team builds analytics agents in Foundry. The business builds service agents in Copilot Studio. Business data lives in Dataverse. Without standard connections, each team copies data or writes one-off APIs. Standard protocols let each agent use the others’ tools safely, with security and governance still in place.

How it works

1. Foundry vs Copilot Studio.

NeedBetter fit
Low-code building, topics, Teams and Microsoft 365 channels, maker ownershipCopilot Studio
Choice of models, custom orchestration in code, evaluation pipelines, deep Azure integrationMicrosoft Foundry
Both: maker front door with specialist code-first agents behind itCopilot Studio agent connected to Foundry agents

2. Power Platform MCP servers. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard. An MCP server lists tools. An agent discovers them and calls them. Dataverse can act as an MCP server at the environment endpoint https://yourorg.crm.dynamics.com/api/mcp. An admin must enable the server and allow the clients that may use it. Its tools include search_data, read_query (SQL SELECT queries), create_record, update_record, describe and table tools such as create_table. Delete tools need explicit user approval. Microsoft notes that tool names can change, so avoid hard-coding them. Usage can consume Copilot Credits depending on licensing.

In Foundry you add an MCP tool to the agent. Its main settings are server_url, server_label, require_approval, an optional allowed_tools list and a project_connection_id that stores authentication.

tool = MCPTool(
    server_label="dataverse",
    server_url="https://yourorg.crm.dynamics.com/api/mcp",
    require_approval="always",
    allowed_tools=["search_data", "read_query"],
    project_connection_id=DATAVERSE_CONNECTION)

With require_approval set to always, the run returns approval requests that your code must approve before a tool call proceeds. This is a human-in-the-loop safety net.

3. Connecting agents to Copilot Studio agents. On the Agents page of a Copilot Studio agent you can add other agents:

TypeStatus (at time of writing)
Child agents inside the same agentGenerally available
Other Copilot Studio agents in the environmentGenerally available
Agents over the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocolGenerally available
Microsoft Foundry agentsPreview
Microsoft 365 Agents SDK agents, Fabric data agentsPreview

For a Foundry agent you pick a connection to the Foundry project, then give a name, a description and the agent ID. The description matters most: generative orchestration reads it to decide when to route to that agent. The Foundry agent must expose the endpoint that Copilot Studio uses, so check the prerequisites first.

4. Work IQ. Work IQ is the intelligence layer that grounds Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents in work context: mail, meetings, files, chats and business systems. It is offered as MCP servers in the Agent 365 tools catalog, including servers for Mail, Calendar, Teams, SharePoint and Dataverse and Dynamics 365. Foundry also has a Work IQ tool in preview. Key rules:

  • Requests run on behalf of the signed-in user. App-only access is not supported, so users only reach data they can already see.
  • Admins govern which servers are allowed in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
  • Licensing depends on the path: a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence or usage-based Copilot Credits billing.

5. Copilot Studio client library. Part of the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK, available for .NET, JavaScript and Python. Your app starts a conversation with a published Copilot Studio agent and sends questions. You need the agent’s connection details from the Channels page (or environment ID and schema name), and an Entra app registration with the delegated Power Platform API permission CopilotStudio.Copilots.Invoke. The agent must use Microsoft authentication or manual authentication, not no authentication. In .NET the main class is CopilotClient, with methods such as StartConversationAsync and AskQuestionAsync.

// simplified from the official sample
await foreach (var a in client.StartConversationAsync(true, ct))
    Show(a);
await foreach (var a in client.AskQuestionAsync("Status of ticket 1042?", conversationId, ct))
    Show(a);

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The data team builds Ticket Analyst in Foundry. It finds trends, such as a spike in Wi-Fi tickets in one building.
  2. They add the Dataverse MCP server as a tool with allowed_tools limited to read tools, and approval set to always during testing.
  3. In Copilot Studio, Help Desk Assistant adds Ticket Analyst from the Agents page. Description: “Answers trend and statistics questions about many tickets, such as counts by category or building over time.”
  4. A student asks the assistant a simple status question; the assistant answers itself. A manager asks “Which building had the most network tickets this month?”; the assistant routes to Ticket Analyst.
  5. The staff dashboard code app is extended with a small .NET service that uses the Copilot Studio client library, so staff can ask Help Desk Assistant questions from inside the dashboard.
  6. For “What did the facilities manager email me about room B12?”, a Work IQ tool answers with the staff member’s own mailbox permissions.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking MCP copies data into the agent. The agent calls tools at run time; Dataverse security still applies.
  • Leaving every MCP tool available. Limit tools and require approval for anything that writes or deletes.
  • Writing vague descriptions for connected agents, so the orchestrator routes to the wrong one.
  • Expecting Work IQ to run with app-only permissions. It is delegated, on behalf of the user.
  • Using the client library against an agent set to no authentication. The SDK path needs authenticated agents.

How the exam asks about it

lessons.title: Dataverse events and data synchronization
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dataverse can publish events to systems outside it. You register a service endpoint (webhook, Azure Service Bus queue or topic, or Azure Event Hub) with the Plug-in Registration Tool, then register steps that post the execution context there. In a plug-in you can post on demand with IServiceEndpointNotificationService.

  • Change tracking lets an external system ask “what changed since last time?” with RetrieveEntityChanges or a Web API delta link.
  • Alternate keys identify rows by business values, such as an external ticket number, instead of GUIDs.
  • UpsertRequest creates the row if the key is new or updates it if it exists, in one call.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dataverse rarely lives alone. Other systems need to know when a ticket changes, and other systems send data in. This lesson covers both directions.

Outbound events: Dataverse posts a message to a destination you register, called a service endpoint. It is like a doorbell that rings in another building when someone enters yours.

Synchronization: an external system asks “what changed since I last looked?” (change tracking) and writes data back using its own identifiers (alternate keys and upsert). It is like a librarian who keeps a bookmark and only reads the new pages.

Why it matters

Polling every row every hour is slow and burns API capacity. Copying data by GUID fails because the other system does not know Dataverse GUIDs. Events and sync features solve both problems with less code and fewer calls. The exam tests whether you pick the right listener and the right sync tool.

How it works

1. Service endpoints and listeners. You register endpoints with the Plug-in Registration Tool, then register steps (message, table, stage, mode) on them, just like plug-in steps. Dataverse sends the execution context: the message, target, images and user information.

EndpointHow it listensChoose it when
WebhookHTTP POST to a URL you own, such as an Azure FunctionYou want a simple HTTP handler and no messaging service
Service Bus queueMessages wait until one consumer reads themOne reliable processor; the listener can be offline for a while
Service Bus topicEach subscription gets its own copySeveral independent subscribers
Event HubHigh-throughput event streamLarge volumes for analytics or telemetry
Relay (one-way, two-way, REST)Listener must be online to receiveRare, older scenarios needing a live listener

For Azure endpoints you supply a SAS connection string and a message format: .NET binary, JSON or XML. Choose JSON for non-.NET consumers. Webhooks support authentication with an HTTP header, a webhook key or a query string value.

Register steps as asynchronous in most cases. Async posts run as system jobs and are retried if the endpoint is unavailable. A synchronous step makes the user wait, and a failure can fail the whole operation.

2. Posting from a plug-in. Sometimes you only want to post when your code decides. Get IServiceEndpointNotificationService from the service provider and call Execute with a reference to the registered endpoint:

var context = (IPluginExecutionContext)
    serviceProvider.GetService(typeof(IPluginExecutionContext));
var notify = (IServiceEndpointNotificationService)
    serviceProvider.GetService(typeof(IServiceEndpointNotificationService));
if (IsSlaBreached(context))
{
    string reply = notify.Execute(
        new EntityReference("serviceendpoint", endpointId), context);
}

The endpoint ID usually comes from the step’s configuration string, read in the plug-in constructor. Credentials stay in the endpoint registration, not in code.

3. Change tracking. Turn on Track changes in the table properties. Then a client asks for changes since a token.

  • SDK: RetrieveEntityChangesRequest with EntityName, Columns, PageInfo and DataVersion (empty the first time). The response’s EntityChanges holds Changes and a DataToken you save for next time.
  • Web API: send Prefer: odata.track-changes on a GET. The last page includes @odata.deltaLink. Calling that link later returns changed rows and deleted rows (marked as deleted entities).
var req = new RetrieveEntityChangesRequest {
    EntityName = "chd_ticket",
    Columns = new ColumnSet("chd_title", "chd_status"),
    PageInfo = new PagingInfo { Count = 500, PageNumber = 1 },
    DataVersion = savedToken };
var resp = (RetrieveEntityChangesResponse)service.Execute(req);
foreach (var c in resp.EntityChanges.Changes)
    if (c.Type == ChangeType.NewOrUpdated) Save(((NewOrUpdatedItem)c).NewOrUpdatedEntity);
    else Remove(((RemovedOrDeletedItem)c).RemovedItem);
savedToken = resp.EntityChanges.DataToken;

4. Alternate keys. An alternate key is one or more columns whose values must be unique, backed by a unique index. Only some column types can be used, such as text, whole number, decimal, date and time, lookup and choice. After you create the key, Dataverse builds the index in the background. Status moves from Pending to Active, or Failed if duplicates already exist. With a key you can address rows without GUIDs: /api/data/v9.2/chd_tickets(chd_externalref='SIS-1042'). You can also bind lookups by key.

5. Upsert. UpsertRequest creates the row if no match exists, or updates it if one does. The response’s RecordCreated tells you which happened.

var t = new Entity("chd_ticket", "chd_externalref", "SIS-1042");
t["chd_title"] = "Projector not working";
var r = (UpsertResponse)service.Execute(new UpsertRequest { Target = t });
Console.WriteLine(r.RecordCreated ? "Created" : "Updated");

In the Web API, a PATCH to a key URL is an upsert. Add If-Match: * to allow update only, or If-None-Match: * to allow create only.

Remember: change tracking answers “what changed in Dataverse?” for outbound sync. Alternate keys and upsert answer “how do I write in without knowing GUIDs?” for inbound sync.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The university’s student information system (SIS) creates maintenance tickets with its own IDs such as SIS-1042. You add the text column chd_externalref and an alternate key on it.
  2. An hourly job sends batches of upserts. New SIS tickets are created; existing ones are updated. No GUID lookups are needed.
  3. Finance, facilities and the reporting service all need escalation events. You register a Service Bus endpoint for a topic with JSON format. Each system has its own subscription.
  4. Your Priority plug-in from lesson D.9 calls IServiceEndpointNotificationService only when it raises Priority to High, so ordinary edits send nothing.
  5. The campus data warehouse uses change tracking. Each night it calls the saved delta link and copies only changed and deleted tickets.
  6. A simple HTTP webhook to the Azure Function from lesson D.12 handles closed tickets and sends a satisfaction survey link.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a queue when several systems each need every message. That needs a topic.
  • Registering endpoint steps as synchronous without reason, which slows users and can block saves.
  • Using an alternate key before its status is Active.
  • Forgetting to save the new data token or delta link after each sync, which causes repeated or missed changes.
  • Putting Service Bus keys in plug-in code instead of the endpoint registration.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Several consumers” → topic. “One processor, may be offline” → queue. “Massive stream for analytics” → Event Hub. “HTTP endpoint we own” → webhook.
  • “Post only when code decides” → IServiceEndpointNotificationService in a plug-in.
  • “Only changes since last sync” → change tracking, RetrieveEntityChanges or a delta link.
  • “External ID, create or update in one call” → alternate key plus UpsertRequest.

terms.definition: A registered destination (Service Bus, Event Hub or webhook) that Dataverse can post the execution context to.

One or more columns that uniquely identify a row, backed by a unique index.
Create or update in one operation, based on the primary or alternate key.

lessons.examTip: “Many subscribers” → Service Bus topic. “Very high volume telemetry or analytics stream” → Event Hub. “Your own HTTP endpoint, no Azure messaging” → webhook. “Only rows changed since last sync” → change tracking.

lessons.title: Custom connectors
lessons.summaryHtml:
A custom connector wraps a REST API so apps, flows and agents can use it like any built-in connector. It is described by an OpenAPI 2.0 definition plus connection settings.

  • Authentication: no authentication, Basic, API key or OAuth 2.0 (generic, Microsoft Entra ID or specific providers).
  • You can build it from blank, import an OpenAPI file or URL or a Postman collection, create it from an Azure service such as Azure Functions or API Management, or import a sample from GitHub.
  • Policy templates change requests and responses without code, for example Set HTTP Header, Set Host URL or Route Request.
  • x-ms extensions improve the designer experience, and custom code in C# can transform requests and responses.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Power Platform has many built-in connectors, but not one for your university’s own systems. A custom connector is a wrapper you build around any REST API. After that, makers use it in canvas apps, cloud flows and Copilot Studio agents like any other connector.

Think of a travel adapter. The API is a foreign socket. The custom connector is the adapter that lets every Power Platform plug fit, with the right shape, voltage and safety switch.

A custom connector has three parts: the API definition (OpenAPI 2.0, describing operations), connection settings (host and authentication) and optional behaviour (policies and custom code).

Why it matters

Without a connector, makers call APIs with raw HTTP actions, copy keys into flows and guess at JSON. A connector hides that. It gives friendly names, dropdowns, one secure connection per user and governance through data policies, because a custom connector can be classified like any other connector. It also becomes reusable across apps, flows and agents, and it travels in a solution.

How it works

1. Ways to create one.

Start fromWhen to use it
BlankSmall API with no definition file; you add actions by hand
OpenAPI file or URLThe API already publishes an OpenAPI 2.0 (Swagger) definition
Postman collectionThe team documents the API in Postman
Azure serviceThe API is an Azure Function or sits behind Azure API Management
GitHubStart from a sample in Microsoft’s open-source connector repository

Developers can also manage connectors from the command line, for example with the pac CLI connector commands or the older paconn tool, which suits source control and pipelines.

2. Authentication.

TypeNotes
No authenticationPublic APIs only
BasicUser name and password per connection
API keyKey sent in a header or query string; you set the label, name and location
OAuth 2.0Generic OAuth 2, Microsoft Entra ID, or specific providers; each user signs in

OAuth needs a client ID, client secret, authorization URL, token URL and refresh URL. The client credentials grant is not supported. If an API only accepts client credentials, put something in front of it, such as an Azure Function or API Management, that handles that flow. Keep an eye on expiring secrets.

3. Azure Functions behind a connector. A common developer pattern: write the logic in an HTTP-triggered Azure Function, then expose it as a connector. With function-level authorization, callers send the function key, for example in the x-functions-key header, so the connector uses API key authentication. For Entra-protected functions, use OAuth 2.0 with Microsoft Entra ID.

4. Policy templates. Policies change requests or responses at run time with no code. Examples include Set HTTP Header, Set Host URL (build the host from a connection parameter, for per-customer URLs) and Route Request (send an operation to a different path). Others set query string parameters or reshape arrays and objects. Policies can use expressions that reference parameters.

5. Extending the OpenAPI definition. Microsoft’s x-ms- extensions shape the maker experience:

  • x-ms-summary: friendly display name for a parameter or field.
  • x-ms-visibility: important (always shown), advanced (hidden under a menu) or internal (hidden from users).
  • x-ms-dynamic-values: dropdown filled by another operation.
  • x-ms-dynamic-schema: the shape of a body or response depends on another operation.
  • x-ms-trigger: marks an operation as a trigger for flows.
"name": "department",
"in": "query",
"type": "string",
"x-ms-summary": "Department",
"x-ms-visibility": "important",
"x-ms-dynamic-values": {
  "operationId": "ListDepartments",
  "value-path": "code",
  "value-title": "name" }

6. Custom code. When policies are not enough, add C# code on the Code page. You write one class named Script that inherits ScriptBase and overrides ExecuteAsync. this.Context gives you the Request, the OperationId, a Logger and SendAsync to call the backend. Only one script per connector is allowed, only some namespaces are supported, and the script must finish within the documented time limit.

public class Script : ScriptBase
{
    public override async Task<HttpResponseMessage> ExecuteAsync()
    {
        var response = await this.Context.SendAsync(
            this.Context.Request, this.CancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
        if (this.Context.OperationId != "GetStaff") return response;
        var body = JObject.Parse(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());
        body["fullName"] = body["firstName"] + " " + body["lastName"];
        response.Content = new StringContent(body.ToString(),
            Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");
        return response;
    }
}
Watch out: when code is enabled it takes precedence over the codeless definition for the operations it handles. Test both paths after enabling it.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The Campus Directory API is an Azure Function app with GetStaff and ListDepartments. It uses function keys.
  2. In the Campus Help Desk solution you create the Campus Directory API connector from the Azure service option, or from its OpenAPI file.
  3. Security: API key, label “Function key”, name x-functions-key, location Header.
  4. Definition: the department parameter on SearchStaff gets x-ms-dynamic-values from ListDepartments, so makers pick from a list. Internal paging parameters get x-ms-visibility: internal.
  5. Policy: Set HTTP Header adds x-client: campus-help-desk so the API team can trace calls.
  6. Code: the Script class adds fullName to GetStaff responses, because the backend only returns first and last names.
  7. Use: the escalation flow calls GetStaff to find the ticket creator’s department, and Help Desk Assistant adds the connector as a tool to answer “Who is my department’s IT contact?”

Common mistakes

  • Importing an OpenAPI 3.0 file and expecting it to work unchanged; custom connectors use OpenAPI 2.0.
  • Choosing OAuth 2.0 for an API that only supports client credentials.
  • Writing custom code for something a policy template already does, such as adding a header.
  • Forgetting that custom code runs for every operation unless you check OperationId.
  • Creating the connector outside a solution, then struggling to move it between environments.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Add or change a header, host or route without code” → policy template.
  • “Dropdown from the API” → x-ms-dynamic-values. “Hide a parameter from makers” → x-ms-visibility internal.
  • “Transform the response in ways policies cannot” → custom code with Script and ExecuteAsync.
  • “Business logic hosted in Azure, used by makers” → Azure Function exposed through a custom connector.

terms.definition: A JSON or YAML description of an API’s operations, parameters and responses; custom connectors use OpenAPI 2.0.
A codeless rule that modifies requests or responses at run time, such as setting a header or routing to a new URL.
OpenAPI extension that marks a parameter or operation as important, advanced or internal in the designer.
OpenAPI extension that fills a parameter’s dropdown from another operation’s results.
A C# class named Script that inherits ScriptBase and overrides ExecuteAsync to transform traffic.

lessons.examTip: “Transform without code” → policy template. “Dropdown filled from the API” → x-ms-dynamic-values. “Logic that policies cannot express” → custom code. “Client credentials only API” → wrap it, because custom connectors do not support that grant type.
